An earlier round built this, saw it change nothing on sets where the stretched finder was never found, and removed it. Behind the wider window it gains 20 renders at 40-50 % (377 → 397 of 400).

  Its first form divided a line the frame takes as flat by the mean of all four sizes, and 15 of 4,000 binarized keystone renders that had read then failed: one line's whole-pixel runs were all one size, the other line's far end was 40 % larger, and that end, inside the flat line's mean, put a version 40 two versions short. Each line now divides by its own sizes whenever the frame is not the parallelogram, and by the mean of four only where it is, so every flat render stays as it was. The timing match searches around the same count. When shipped it lost one binarized render of 4,000, a version 28 at 2.3 px/module whose whole-pixel runs are ±9 % of the size, where neither estimate is the dimension (the mean says 134, the lines 138 and 134, the symbol is 129).

- Past 30 % keystone a triangle's shape cannot pick the triple, but the number of rows confirming each finder can. With every finder found, the selection failed: the stretched finder's row-scan size is up to twice the others', so the size spread that keeps false triples out penalized the real triple more than a false candidate inside the symbol, which also makes the better triangle with two real finders. The drawn triple ranked anywhere from second to 142nd.

  A finder's centre band is three modules tall whatever perspective does to its shape, and few rows repeat a false candidate. Ordered by the height (rows over module size) over which their least confirmed member was seen, the drawn triple came first after the selected one in every failing render. That order cannot replace the selection (three well-confirmed finders from two symbols are its best triple), so its first triple is decoded only after the selected one fails, and only once its two timing patterns read through its own frame. Through their frames the drawn triples read no timing module wrong. Triples holding a false candidate read 20 to 49 % wrong.

  Where the stride pass selected and returned, the list counts each finder on a third of its rows, once or twice, so the order is coarse. Three renders in 1,600 needed the second triple, so a failed decode verifies two. Verifying eight or 64 read none more. Sweeping the skipped rows before ordering made the first triple enough but doubled the benchmark's 740 × 740 noise (3.1 to 6.2 ms), as every failing attempt then paid for a sweep. The 512 × 512 noise it was first timed on, from another generator, did not show this. zxing-cpp keeps up to 256 triples in order of their longer leg and decodes each in turn.

  With this alone switched off, 30-40 % falls from 400 to 392, 40-50 % from 397 to 383 and 20-30 % at 2-3 px/module from 390 to 382. It also gave the four grey keystone renders of 4,000 gained below 20 %.

- A triangle's shape names the corner only while its hypotenuse is its longest side. The timing patterns always name it. Tilted about both axes toward the top-left finder, a plane draws that finder nearest and the finderless corner farthest, and past about 43 % keystone a leg of the image triangle outgrows its hypotenuse (1.10 times it at 50 % on version 40. Along an axis the leg never passes 0.82 of it). The vertex opposite the longest side, the rule every reader in `.references` uses, is then another finder, and every size, dimension and grid after it is built on the wrong corner. Toward a corner at 40-50 % keystone, 24 of 400 renders failed this way, each of which reads through its drawn grid. The count did not fail: from the wrong corner the estimate stayed within 3.2 modules of the dimension, and the timing patterns read in none of the 37 renders tilted toward a corner or in any direction. zxing-cpp weighs each side by the ratio of its two finders' sizes, its repair for a sample of this kind. With the near finder at the corner, both legs have the large end, and they grow.

  Three centres cannot identify the corner, since a projective map can put a triangle's right angle at any vertex. Only the true corner has both timing patterns running from it: from either other vertex one line crosses the data, and on flat symbols of versions 2, 25 and 40 neither reads. So when the shape's corner neither reads nor gives a verdict on the content, each other corner is decoded once its timing patterns read through its own frame, and an alternative triple picks its corner the same way, the shape's corner first. A read from the shape's corner costs nothing more.

  Toward a corner, 40-50 % went from 373 to 398 of 400, and in any direction from 385 to 398. The corpus's `qrcode-2/fix-finderpattern-order.webp` reads at all four turns, and no other envelope cell, sweep or corpus image moved. Switching off the selected triple's other corners alone loses all of the envelope's gain and the photograph. The alternatives' corner reads 19 more of 2,000 renders tilted toward the top-left finder at 40-50 % (10 at 2-3 px/module). Without the timing check first, every failed triple would pay two more decodes, 70-80 % on a failure.

  A content verdict from the shape's corner ends the triple, as a read does. Decoded from their two wrong corners, the drawn triples of 116,948 renders (versions 1-40, flat, keystoned to 30 % and tilted 44-50 % toward the top-left finder) gave 233,896 failures and nothing past Reed-Solomon. So a verdict there needs the same event that would give a read, and guarding the verdict alone would add a path nothing reaches.

- Whole-pixel runs cannot hold the 1:1:3:1:1 ratio on grey edges at about 2 px/module, and loosening the ratio is the wrong repair. An anti-aliased or resampled edge leaves a grey pixel, and whichever side of the threshold it falls on, the run is a pixel off its module. A 2.1 px light module covering 0.55 + 1 + 0.55 of three pixels reads 1 px under a threshold of 144 (Otsu puts it there because the edge greys fall into the dark class and raise its mean), outside the half-module tolerance, so the symbol is `NotDetected`. This hit all three symbologies and the builders' own anti-aliased rounded and circular finder shapes.

  Two other repairs were measured. A tolerance floor of 1.5 px reads those renders, but on 1-2 px noise it filled the candidate list (5 candidates to the cap of 32) and made the single-finder symbologies' failure paths 2-4x slower. Retrying the failed image at twice the size read slightly more and cost every unreadable image 2.5-18x.

  The shipped repair keeps the ratio and changes the measurement. Runs that fail by less than 1.5 px (the same budget on each of the five) are measured again from grey levels, in the row scan and all three cross-checks: each edge moves off its pixel boundary by the coverage of the pixels beside it, and the runs are held to the same half-module tolerance. The dark and light levels are the means of each threshold class's outer half, since the inner halves are the edge pixels being measured. An image with no pixel between the two levels would measure as its whole pixels did, so the second look is off for it, and two-level noise and crisp renders scan as before, candidate for candidate. From about 2.9 px/module the outer runs' half-module tolerance is the wider, so a finder there is never re-measured. On the three-module centre run the strict tolerance is wider at every supported density, so a window failing the strict check on its centre is never re-measured.

  The remaining cost is on grey texture with no symbol (blurred 1 px noise at 512 px: 1.1 to 2.1 ms `NotDetected`). It comes from the near-miss test on every window, not the measurement, and two restructurings did not move it.

  The near-miss tolerance is an absolute number of pixels, so the centre run gets the same budget as the outer ones, not three times it. Scaling it by run width, as the strict check scales its per-module tolerance, made a 1:1:1:1:1 run a near miss, and the review round measured it admitting a cross whose two axes read 1:1:3:1:1 and whose diagonal does not. The cross was still admitted afterwards, mostly not by the second look but by the diagonal's own ratio (next item).

- A finder's centre is the same share of every line through it, and the falling diagonal is held to that. A cross whose row and column carry the finder's runs and whose falling diagonal has a one-module centre passed the ratio on that diagonal: equal runs miss the tolerance by a tenth of a module on the centre, and the 45° walk adds the corner pixels beside it to the run. Over 10,496 anti-aliased renders of that cross at 2 to 4 px/module, 256 sub-pixel offsets each, the whole-pixel scan made it a candidate in 4,050 and the grey levels in 4,468. From 2.25 px/module up the two agreed. Below it the grey levels added 418, mostly through the axis cross-checks, which read the cross's bars correctly, and through the diagonal's coverage only at 2.0 px/module. The review's reading, that the coverage measurement admitted it by crossing module corners, held only for that last slice.

  The rising diagonal now also has to read when the falling diagonal's centre is under four fifths of the mean share the row's and column's centres are of their lines, on rows of 2 px modules or more (`IsDiagonalCentreShort`). Every line through concentric squares, or through an affine image of them, crosses the rings in the same proportions, and a thin or thick print moves every line's centre alike. The cross went from 4,468 candidates to 44. No read moved over 624 real images and the image decode sweep (54,400, 18,400 and 29,440 renders). The rule fired on 51 of 14,400 renders of a lone finder printed up to a fifth of a module thin or thick, or turned, and the rising diagonal read every one. Two-level noise went from 459 candidates to 439, and from 62 images yielding a triple to 59. 8-bit noise did not change.

  These were measured and not taken:

  - The rising diagonal on every candidate: noise down to 76 candidates, but three real images lost.
  - A fixed share instead of the axes' (a falling diagonal centre under 2.5 of its 7 modules): the cross down to 13, but two renders of a finder printed a fifth of a module thin lost.
  - The axes' share without the 2 px floor: four anti-aliased renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module lost, outside the envelope.
  - Refusing a candidate whose two diagonals both have a centre under 2.5 of 7 modules: the cross with both diagonals dotted from 4,505 to 22, but five anti-aliased renders of a real finder lost.

  A cross with both diagonals dotted still passes in 3,470 of 10,496 renders, because its rising diagonal reads as its falling one does. Like the one-diagonal cross, it stays a candidate and does not become a read:
  - Drawn alone at 2 to 4 px/module, neither cross was read by any of the three decoders, and neither was a lone real finder (0 of 336 renders each).
  - Beside a symbol, past its quiet zone (to the right, below, off the corner) at 2.5 to 5 px/module, every symbol read correctly with either cross there, as with a real finder there or nothing (720 Standard QR, 360 Micro QR and 360 rMQR renders per shape).
  - Inside a symbol's data it was not measured on its own. Random data with three planted finders kept every triple right.

- Between 1 and 1.5 px/module a crisp symbol holds all its information, but nothing built on ratios or finder centres reads it. A crisp render at a fractional scale, the builders' own or any nearest-neighbour resize, draws each module 1 or 2 px wide, a whole pixel or more, but two things the decoders rely on stop working. A run is up to a whole module off, so the 1:1:3:1:1 check's half-module tolerance refuses most finders (`NotDetected` on 57-73 % of crisp renders), with no grey to measure instead. A sample has (pitch − 1) / 2 to spare, an eighth of a pixel at 1.25 px/module, while finder centres are good only to half a pixel, so every grid extrapolated from a centre fails in the data. Both repairs read edges instead of measuring sizes.

  The finder is accepted as a whole pattern: its runs must have the shape a small crisp finder leaves (four runs of 1 or 2 px around one of 3 to 5), repeated pixel for pixel on a neighbouring row, and then all 49 modules are read through the six edges the row and column measured. That is exact where three ratios are not, and over 18 two-level noise images it admits no candidate the ratio scan did not. The shape test checks the centre run first because on fine noise it runs on every window, and the row comparison keeps noise from reaching the cross-checks. A render that passes the ratio is still accepted the old way, on three lines through the centre, so a finder with one ring module wrong is refused only where the ratio fails it. The column is held to the same window as in the ratio path, but the rising diagonal is not asked of a whole pattern: the 49 modules include every light-ring module that diagonal crosses. Asking it anyway refused no broken ring more, and lost real stretched finders at 1.25 × 1.6-1.75 px, where a whole-pixel walk at 45° crosses module corners.

  The grid is not fitted (`ModuleBoundaryReader`, shared by the three symbologies). A timing pattern crosses every module boundary past the finder, and a finder's centre line crosses four of its own. The two boundaries inside a three-module run (a finder's centre square, an rMQR alignment or corner pattern on the timing row) show in the modules in line with it, because a crisp module has no edge inside it. Each module is read at the middle pixel of the cell its boundaries frame, however wide it came out. A least-squares fit fills only the boundaries nothing crossed, and a line that does not read as a timing pattern refuses the whole table. While a module is at most 2 px, run lengths classify a run: one module is 1-2 px, three are 3-6, seven are 7 or more. So the single-module bound is 1.2 times the finder's module size, not the 1.6 of the fitted timing lines (at 1.6 a three-pixel alignment run on an rMQR timing row counted as one module, and the width came out two short). A least-squares grid through the same boundaries, tried first, left about a tenth of the renders below 1.25 px/module unread. The table leaves none.

  The table applies below 1.75 px/module, measured at the finder, on symbols along the image axes (any right angle, mirrored or not). For Standard QR and rMQR it comes before the fitted grids there (Micro QR tries its fitted frames first, and their corners held in every builder render): where both read, the table's corners are the symbol's own edges while the fitted grids' are extrapolated to within a module, and for rMQR the perspective search could otherwise spend the whole attempt budget first. The table does not read anti-aliased input at this density, where a module centre covers well under half of any pixel. The coverage reading through the grey-level frame (below) reads some of it, 356 of 2,400 sweep renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module where 36 read before, and it stays outside the envelope.

- Measure between edges of the same polarity. The module size used to be the finder's outer-to-outer span through its center (7 modules), but grey edge pixels on one side of the threshold move a dark-to-light and a light-to-dark edge in opposite directions, so that span included both shifts. One pixel of ink spread at 3 px/module is +4.8 %, 4.8 modules over a version 24 span, and v20-v37 read one or two versions low (lighter edges read them high). The error is an asymmetry, not noise, so averaging more such spans does not remove it. The dark ring's inner edge on one side and outer edge on the other are 6 modules apart whatever the bloom. Pairing them twice per line took the mean error from +0.4..+1.4 % to within ±0.3 %. It does not narrow the spread from pixel quantization along a rotated ray (still about 5.6 % at 3 px/module), which is why the version information is also read.

- A ring printed or read too thick or too thin keeps the distances between its like edges, and the cross-checks read them. Ink spread, a thin print, a blurred ring cut by one threshold, and a screen's glow read inverted all move every dark edge of a finder the same way, so its dark runs are all longer or all shorter than their modules and the line's own 1:1:3:1:1 check refuses it, most often on a diagonal (3, 7, 13, 6, 3 px at 5 px/module). The distance from each edge to the next same-polarity edge stays 2, 4, 4 and 2 modules. A cross-check line the ratio refuses is read by those four distances, each held to half a module (the ratio's own margin), with the fitted shift under half a module a run and a module of at least 2 px.

  Candidates on 540 two-level noise images changed as the conditions were added:

  - Read this way on every line, the row scan included, with the shift allowed up to a whole module and no floor: from 442 to 1,220.
  - With the bound and the floor, the row scan keeping the ratio (so the same windows reach the cross-checks), and a line's shift held to the row's sign (one print or one blur moves a finder's edges one way): 518.
  - With a finder any of whose lines needed like edges also reading its rising diagonal (a real ring is closed): 459.

  The walk's side cap allows these lines the largest ratios their conditions permit: a side run under 16/19 of the centre and a third of the total, which on the column never passes the ratio's own cap. A correct but looser cap, 25/19 of the centre, made successful reads 4 to 5 % slower. The tight one costs about 3 % at most. The centre bound did not grow: these lines' centres are 0.28 to 0.57 of the total up to 90 px, inside the ratio's 0.21 to 0.64.

  Against the decoder before it, the results were:

  - Real images: 391 to 401 of 548, none lost.
  - The synthetic sweeps: identical, but for one render gained.
  - Symbols whose dark edges all moved by 0.1 to 0.24 of a module: 1,260 to 1,702 of 2,400, one lost.
  - Binarized renders, flat, keystoned to 20 % and tilted to 50 %: +110, +127 and +127 of 4,000 each, with 3 tilted ones lost.
  - At 40-50 % keystone: +1 and −2 of 800, one of them traced to a false candidate in the data that now completes a better triangle.

  These were not taken:

  - The runs corrected by the fitted shift and held to the ratio (16 more real-image reads, 1,270 noise candidates).
  - The distances held to half a module per module of distance (+10 net, 8,659 noise candidates).
  - A 2.5 px floor (loses `qrcode-3/30`).
  - Separate caps for light and dark side runs (16/19 and 4/13, 5/7 and 1/3, no faster than the one cap).
  - The like-edge module size for the candidate (no read moved).

  The rising diagonal costs one read, `qrcode-3/30` at 270°.

  A finder whose every row misses the ratio, as a uniform spread along the image axes draws it, is still not found. With the row scan also reading like edges, the shifted symbols read 1,841 of those 2,400 instead of 1,702, but noise gave 471 candidates, failures ran 11 % slower on the same row kernel, and a knife-edge photograph was lost, so it is a lead whose cost in the edge-list kernel is to be measured first. The ring's closure, which another reader checks once its run tests pass, was the lead for a finder lost near 2 px/module. The corpus had none, and it was not taken.

- A symbol's stated version beats an estimate of it. Versions 7+ carry their version twice, BCH(18,6)-protected, each copy within 7 modules of a finder, and since the grid is anchored on the finder centers, a matrix sampled at a dimension several modules off still reads them (4 modules off at version 27 moves them a quarter of a module). The image path reads them from the failed sampling and tries the dimension they name before the runner-up. Near the axis at 3 px/module the estimate was measured up to 9 modules off. The snap is clamped to versions 1-40, because an estimate just past 177 modules used to round to 41 and come back `NotDetected`.

  Reading the blocks through the first transform before sampling, to verify a triple, was analysed and closed without being built (2026-09-28). Through a grid anchored on the finder centres, a dimension Δ modules off moves a block about 7·Δ / (dim − 7) modules, a whole module at Δ = 16 near version 30, so that read misses where the count is far enough off to need it. The blocks are 5 to 7 modules from their nearest finder, whose own axes and sizes would place them. The case it was for, a drawn triple whose count lies outside the timing match's ±16 modules, occurred in none of 40,000 envelope renders and none of the corpus gap, and the 47 renders whose drawn triple is not verified also read their version blocks right through the first transform, so a dimension-independent read would add nothing. As a triple check it is weak: a copy within 3 errors of a codeword is about 13 % of random 18-bit words. Rejecting a triple whose version disagrees with its count was not taken either, because `TimingPatternsRead` already refuses false alternatives and a real symbol whose version blocks alone are damaged still decodes through the timing dimension.

- The alignment checks had been calibrated on the biased module size. Correcting it turned 11 rotated renders from reading to failing, all in the alignment search, whose result changed when the module size moved by under 1 %. Three defects stacked:

  - The search took the first hit in scan order, so a false pattern to the left won while the real one sat 0.1 px from the prediction on the same row.
  - It compared each run with the plain module size, although at 45° a row's run through a module is √2 times longer.
  - Each run on its own gained or lost the bloom pixel: at 3 px/module and 45° a light run measured 2 px against an expected 4.2.

  The search now keeps the hit nearest the prediction and re-centers it on its own row (row hits near the pattern's edge cut its center short and lean toward the prediction), derives the expected run length per scan direction from the grid axes, and checks each light run plus the dark center as a pair (same polarity again). It requires the light ring at ±1 module as well as the dark ring at ±2, because data around a real pattern was measured passing everything else 1.8 modules from it. On three sweeps the strict light ring beat both requiring at least 6 of 8 and requiring none.

- An anchor's resolution must be weighed against how far the transform extrapolates from it. At about 2 px/module the alignment pattern's centre is the midpoint of a 1-2 px run, resolved to a third of a module (found at 44.00 against a true 43.64), while the finder centres, 7 modules across, were within 0.14 px. The four-point transform reads that third of a module as perspective and extends it across the bottom-right block, putting 17 to 22 modules wrong on flat level-L renders that the three finders' parallelogram sampled with none wrong. So an alignment-anchored global transform that fails to decode is retried through the finders alone, only on the failure path. A keystoned symbol still decodes through the alignment anchor first.

  A failure-path cost must still be measured on failures. As first shipped, the fallback made the finder-found failures it was measured on 15-40 % slower (damaged data at 2-4 px/module, v2 to v40), because it decoded again where it could not help: at the true size a flat symbol samples identically through both anchors, and at the runner-up the grid is the wrong size either way. Skipping those two cases brought it within 10 % of the decoder without the fallback. This was measured, not reasoned: the first explanation, modules drawn 1 px wide, could not be right, because a non-antialiased fill covers a pixel whose centre lies inside the module, so flooring a true module centre always lands inside it.

- The parallelogram after an anchored grid is also read by coverage, as the four-point and frame grids are. It had been read only one pixel against Otsu, with no measurement behind the difference. A photograph of round finders and small round modules, its alignment pattern drawn as dots, anchors a fifth of a module off. The parallelogram through its finders fails one pixel against Otsu and reads by coverage with no correction, at every right angle. Nothing else in the corpus moved, 13 anti-aliased sweep renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module now read that neither reader read before, and nothing was lost. The cost is one coverage reading on a failing grey-level image whose anchored grid failed (measured 2026-09-28).

- Below 2 px/module a grey-edged symbol fails in its frame, not its pixels, and the grey levels place the frame. Sampled through the geometry they were drawn with, using the decoder's own reader (one pixel against Otsu), anti-aliased renders at 1.25-1.5 px/module read 2,388 of 2,400, where the decoder read 1,367. Its finders were a median 0.22 modules and up to half a module off, because a centre from thresholded runs is good to half a pixel, and the grid extrapolates that error across the symbol.

  A grey edge pixel's level is the share of it the module covers, so the darkness-weighted centroid of a finder's centre square is exact where a run is not (`ConcentricCentroid`). The window runs along the symbol's axes, ± 2 modules, ending inside the light ring, so its edge pixels are light and weigh nothing wherever the edge falls. This cut the error to a median 0.044 modules, and the three finders' parallelogram read 2,261 of the 2,400. The same centroid refines the alignment patterns and mesh nodes (± 1 module), for another 17 anti-aliased reads at 1.25-1.5 px/module and 35 keystoned ones from the mesh nodes, measured before the refinement was limited to grey-level images.

  Three details each cost reads when wrong:

  - The window's scale is each finder's own module size along the finder-to-finder lines. A finder's row runs grow by up to √2 under a turn, and a window scaled by them reached the dark ring and lost 427 turned and keystoned renders. One size for all three lost keystoned renders whose far finder measures 45 % larger than the near one (12 against 5).
  - The centroid takes two passes, the second centring the window. Below 1.6 px/module the light ring is under two pixels, and an off-centre window takes in more of the dark ring on one side (one pass left 11 of 36 test placements more than a tenth of a module off).
  - The module size the dimension estimate divides by is measured again from the refined centres, since the runs are read outward from them (keystone 6-20 %: 2,180 → 2,210 of 2,400).

  The centroid runs only on a grey-level image: on a two-level image the centroid of whole pixels is no finer than the runs, and on a camera-binarized photograph (`qrcode-3/04`) it moved a blobby centre square by 0.85 px and lost the image at all four turns. Binarized images, the regional pass's included, keep their run centres. Refining them too gained 12 real-image reads and 12 keystoned renders but lost that photograph at every turn and another through the regional pass, while refining only grey images loses nothing.

  These were refuted:

  - The whole finder as the window (± 4 modules, the dark ring's edges averaged in), a median 0.073 modules off against 0.044, and 2,096 of 2,400 reads against 2,261.
  - Darkness scaled linearly from the image's extremes instead of the class levels, 0.043 against 0.044, so the levels are not what limits it.
  - The dark area as the module size (√(area / 9)), within 2 % on anti-aliased renders but 15 % either way on crisp ones, where a square in whole pixels is not 9 modules.

  The refined frame costs grey version 40 reads 5 to 6 % (rotated and soft renders).

- One pixel against Otsu is the wrong reader for a grey edge, and the right reader runs as a second reading, not a new first one. On a blurred image Otsu sits above the midpoint of the two levels, because edge greys fall into the dark class, so a light module between dark ones reads dark. The coverage reading (`LuminanceSampler`) compares the luminance interpolated at the module's centre with the midpoint of the two levels. Through the true frame it read 2,399 of 2,400 bilinear upscales at 1.5-2 px/module, against 2,338 for one pixel against Otsu, and through the refined frame 2,399 of the bilinear and 2,367 of the anti-aliased renders at 1.25-1.5 px/module, against 2,336 and 2,261.
- A module is the unit to split light from dark in, where the light changes across the symbol. A threshold over the image, global or regional, is set in pixels, and one level, the coverage read's too, splits every module of the symbol at once. Read in module space (2026-10-12), each module against the mean of the modules around it, the same grids read twelve more of BoofCV's photographs, fifteen more of ZXing's reads and ten more of the corpus's with none lost, and 207 anti-aliased renders at 1.0 to 1.5 px/module, where the read is one pixel against its neighbours' mean. It stays a second reading, as coverage does: the threshold reads two photographs it does not.
- The regional pass had thrown the grey image away. It binarizes to find a symbol the global threshold cannot see, and then read the symbol from that binarization, one pixel a module, as if the grey levels were gone. Handing the pass the image it binarized, with its polarity, lets the grid it places be read from grey levels: seven of the twelve photographs, among them two symbols at 2.3 to 2.4 px/module, `nominal/image004` and ZXing's `qrcode-2/5`, recorded before as anchor precision and as not detected. The gain was measured before the shared pass was touched, with the grey image passed aside in a scratch build, and the interface changed only once it had counted.
- What a probe names is a floor. With another reader's corners as the truth, the decoder's own first grid read three gap photographs in module space; the stage read one of the three as built (`qrcode-4/09`), the second with a window of four modules for three (`curved/image034`), the third only with the grey image at the regional pass (`shadows/image013`), and ten photographs the probe had not named, seven of them outside that reader's gap.
- A finder is a shape, and three shapes fix a plane where three points and a guess do not. The centres of the photographs this stage was built on measured within 0.35 module, and every grid through them and one more point left the far corner 0.4 to 1.5 modules out; the plane fitted to the twelve corners of the finders' inner outlines (2026-10-12) reads fifteen more of BoofCV's photographs, nine more of ZXing's reads and seven more of the corpus's, with none lost. The measurement already existed, for rMQR's single finder, and so did the least-squares plane, for the small mesh: the stage joins the two.
- Another reader's corners are not the truth. On `damaged/image009` the fitted plane put the far corner 0.9 module from go-qr's reported corner and read with 2 to 7 corrections, where the grid through this library's centres and that reported corner did not read. A reader reports where its own model puts the corners, and for a damaged symbol that is an extrapolation like any other; a probe that takes them for the truth measures agreement, not error.
- An anchor helps one symbol and hurts another, so both planes are tried. With the anchor in the fit three photographs under glare read that do not without it; without it two photographs of ZXing's `qrcode-4` set read, fifteen reads over the set and the corpus, that do not with it. The weight the lead gives the anchor, three, read two photographs fewer here than one or two: a constant copied with a technique is measured like the technique.
- A test that reads is not a test of the call it was written for. The first shot chosen for the anchored plane read with that call removed, through the unanchored branch, since blur had hidden the alignment pattern at the pass that read it; six photographs depended on a call no test held. Each call site is switched off alone before its test is believed, and here that found the bent shots for the anchored plane and two real captures for the plane without the anchor.

  It re-reads a grid that failed on a grey-level image, and the result is decoded only when it changes a module. A crisp image has no grey levels and one pixel reads it exactly, and a symbol that reads pays nothing. The limit is the failure path's cost in grids: Micro QR sends about 19,000 grids a failing image through Reed-Solomon, half with a format word within 3 bits, and reading all of those again took 8-bit noise to 1.78x and another symbology's image to 2-5.6x. A real symbol's format modules sit next to its finder, where the frame is best, and texture reads an exact word about 1 time in 1,000, so Micro QR reads a grid again only when its format word read exactly, which keeps 8-bit noise at 1.05x, for 6 of the 284 reads it gained at 1.25-2.5 px/module.

- Once the frame is accurate enough to sample the timing modules, they give the dimension. Blur and a turn break both ways of finding it: the finder runs measure the module size up to about 6 % off (a bilinear version 40 at 1.95 px/module measured 1.83), putting the estimate a version or more out, and at version 40 past the range, while under a turn at 2-2.5 px/module the counted timing runs can stop reading. So through the refined finders the grid of each dimension within four versions of the estimate is sampled along both timing lines, and the dimension leaving under an eighth of their modules wrong is tried where the estimate is refused and the count fails, and after the version information when the estimate's grid fails. The eighth tolerates a few damaged timing modules (four of a version 40's 322 painted over still reads) but not a broken line (a quarter painted over is `NotDetected`, as before). Two versions either way was not enough for the version 36-40 bilinear renders at 1.87-1.94 px/module.

- A blurred finder can be invisible at the global threshold, and the midpoint of the two levels finds it. A 1 px/module image scaled up bilinearly to about 2.45 px/module leaves the finder's light ring as one bright pixel (149, 252, 155 on a Micro QR M1). Otsu at 163, pulled up by the edge greys, makes the ring 1 px wide (runs 3:2:8:1:4), so no candidate is found and the symbol is `NotDetected`. At the midpoint, 146, the runs are 3:2:7:3:2. Micro QR and rMQR scan once more at the midpoint, last, after the regional pass, for each polarity whose strided scan and sweep found no candidate on a grey-level image.

  Both conditions were measured. Gated on no grid reading its format information, the scan ran on every other symbology's image, whose finders are found and fail (rMQR on a Micro QR image up to 2.9x). Gated on no candidate, it costs those images nothing. Placed inside each attempt, it ran on every symbol whose finder a shadow hides from the global threshold, before the regional pass read it (an M1 under a 55 % shadow 11.2 → 14 µs). After the regional pass it costs those nothing either, and the blurred finders it is for were `NotDetected` on `main`, regional pass included. Standard QR has no such scan: its sweep reads 4,799 of the 4,800 bilinear renders at 2-3.5 px/module without it, and the one left fails as it did on `main`.

- Count the modules where the symbol marks them, and measure only where it does not. A renderer that snaps each module to whole pixels draws them 2 or 3 px wide at 2.13 px/module, and a finder that lands on 2 px modules measures 2.0, 6 % off the symbol's pitch: two versions at version 29, too far for the version information to be read. The timing patterns alternate one module at a time between the finders, so their dark runs number 2v + 3 whatever width each module was drawn, and the two lines (row 6 and column 6) must agree. A line whose runs are not all about a module long refuses rather than miscounts, which a single painted-over timing module triggers. The count is a fallback, taken only once the estimate's sampling fails: tried first, it cost every successful decode 8 % for rare renders.

  A fallback must also be reachable from every early exit before it. The estimate refuses a dimension more than four modules past version 40, snapped finders at versions 39-40 measure a few percent small, which put a 177-module symbol there, and the refusal returned before the count ran.

- Use one pixel convention everywhere: integers are pixel edges, and the pixel containing a point is its floor. The finder centres were always in that convention (a run's end index is exclusive), but every sampler, in all three symbologies and both kernels, picked its pixel with `(int)(x + 0.5f)`, which reads half a pixel right of and below each module centre. Two anchors had the opposite half-pixel error and partly cancelled it: the alignment pattern's vertical centre (`+ 0.5` where the run's midpoint needs `+ 1`) and rMQR's sub-finder refinement. At 2.5 px/module and up the offset stays inside the module, so it went unseen. At 1 px/module it reads the neighbouring module every time (Standard QR 0 of 2,560 clean renders, rMQR 4 of 256, Micro QR 41 of 109), and at 1.5-2.2 px/module, where the builder's fixed-size renders land, it reads module edges (288 of 676 fixed-size renders across the three symbologies decoded). After the fix every 1 px/module render reads, and 666 of the 676. The rest were the builder's whole-pixel module snapping, covered by the timing-pattern lesson above.

  The offset also had an effect it should not have had. It points the same way as the finders-only corner's error when the top edge of a keystoned symbol is shorter, so version 1 past its 2 % envelope, and version 2+ with a missing alignment pattern, read further in that one direction (on a 20,000-render sweep, flipping the keystone turned `main`'s 19,871 into 19,721). A version 2 with its alignment pattern erased read at 3 % only with the top edge shrinking. Corrected, the two directions read alike.

- A symbol under a lighting gradient has no global threshold, and the second binarization is an added attempt, not a new first one. On photographs with a shading gradient across the symbol, a light module on the dim side is darker than a dark module on the bright side, so one threshold reads a whole side as one class and the finders there as solid. Every image of one real-image corpus set failed that way, as `NotDetected`.

  A regional binarization reads them (`LocalBinarizer`, the hybrid scheme of ZXing: an 8 × 8 block's black point comes from its mean, or from its neighbours when the block is flat, and each pixel is compared with the mean of the 25 around its block). Replacing the global threshold with it lost 14 reads elsewhere in a probe: it has no grey levels to give the finder's second look, and a block-local threshold moves edges the global one had right. Three binarizations were probed as that fallback on the real images:

  - A local mean over a tenth of the image, 8 % under it.
  - One over an eighth, 5 % under it.
  - The hybrid scheme, which read the most (359 of 548 against 353 and 356) at about half the cost and needs no integral image.

  It matched an independent port of ZXing's `HybridBinarizer` on 20,000 random cases in three SIMD configurations.

  So it runs after both global polarities have failed, in both polarities (`RegionalRetry`), each binarized from its own pixels. The flat-block rule reads a block as paper, and the paper of a light-on-dark symbol is dark, so inverting the positive's regional output reads 2 of 48 such renders, where binarizing the negative reads 44.

  A polarity is decoded only when its regional binarization moves a pixel out of the class its own global threshold put it in. An image of only 0 and 255 is not binarized at all, because every regional threshold then lies in [0, 251], so neither polarity can differ. Both 0/255 noise and a black-and-white crisp symbol that failed on its data pay nothing more. The skip is exact, not tuned. The share of pixels a regional binarization moves does not separate reads from costs: reads range from 0.5 % on Micro QR photographs to 51 % on `qrcode-5`, and inside that range lie 8-bit noise at 0.6 %, another symbology's image at 0.02 to 2.3 % and a textured ramp at 40 %. A count of blocks with a quarter moved does not separate them either, and any bound would have lost reads or kept the cost.

  Any other image pays up to two binarizations, plus a decode for each polarity whose binarization moves a pixel. A binarization takes about 0.09 ms at 512 × 512, and the negative's is skipped once the positive's decode reads. Both are read from the positive, the negative complemented as it loads, and written into the one buffer the inverted retry rented. (Binarized into a second rented buffer, the negative allocated an image-sized array on every failing large image where the shared pool stops at 1 MB: .NET Framework, .NET Core 5 and earlier.) Noise of two levels more than 24 apart moves no pixel, since every block holds both levels and its threshold falls between them. Two levels closer than that make every block flat, which reads the lighter level as paper, and the darker one too unless it is 0. A large flat area of the darker level on the top or left edge, or of a level more than half the lighter one, can also move pixels.

  Against `main` before it, the results were:

  - The real images: 295 → 359 of 548 Standard QR reads (2 of them by the negative) and 60 → 64 of 64 Micro QR, none lost.
  - The synthetic sweep: +400 Standard QR reads (bilinear upscales at 1.5-2 px/module +154, anti-aliased edges at 1.25-2 +103, keystone past 6 % +74), +45 Micro QR (42 of them bilinear at 2-2.5), of which a refusal of regional M1 reads cost 36, leaving 9, until the evidence rule replaced it, and +11 rMQR.

  Gains on evenly lit images come from the same difference: a block-local threshold places grey edge pixels differently, so a symbol one threshold misses by a few edges can read at the other.

  Micro QR's regional pass at first refused, by level, what texture passed as: any M1 read, an empty read that needed correction, an M3-M or M4-M read at its limit. Each refusal cost real reads and left texture landing on the next level. The Micro QR evidence rule replaced them ([microqr-decoder.md](microqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned)): every grid, in every pass, uses only the corrections its structure justifies.

  The cost is up to two more decodes, one per polarity, on a failing image with grey in it: blurred noise, a gradient, another symbology's image, an anti-aliased symbol past correction. The multiple was largest where the global threshold fails cheaply. One threshold splits a ramp with ±20 noise and no symbol into two solid halves in 0.2 ms at 256 px, but under the regional pass the ramp became finder-like specks and cost Micro QR and rMQR 16 to 41 ms (80 to 200 times). ±8 noise leaves every block flat and costs nothing more. A textured ramp holding no symbol went 0.32 → 1.80 ms for Standard QR, and 21 → 88 ms and 25 → 113 ms for Micro QR and rMQR, whose every attempt is a strided finder scan followed, when that fails, by a full sweep.

  The regional attempts keep the sweep, because a strided scan misses a finder whose band falls between the rows it visits. A cut that skipped the sweep there lost 30 to 47 of each 880-render set of unevenly lit Micro QR and rMQR renders at 1.5-2 px/module to their position alone, although every measured set had shown no loss. The synthetic sets that turn a symbol or offset it by fractions of a pixel are evenly lit, so the global attempts, which keep the sweep, read those renders before the regional attempt runs. The unevenly lit set was axis-aligned, and no real image in the corpus had the case. Eight or more finder-like marks are a second case: they outrank the real finder in the strided list, which tries eight (1,254 of 12,288 renders with ten decoys read only with the sweep).

  The finder search's contract is that a decoder's envelope is never narrower than a full sweep's, and cost is not a reason to break it. The single-finder scan departs from it in one place, recorded as a residual: after a read too long for the destination it runs no sweep, so a call probing for its buffer size costs what a sized one does ([single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan)). The failure-path work addressed the cost instead, making failing Micro QR decodes on noise-like images 1.5 to 2.6 times faster and rMQR ones 4.8 to 7.3 times faster, with every result unchanged ([Micro QR](microqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned), [rMQR](rmqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned)).

- Under keystone the fourth anchor fails in its prediction, not its search, and the finders already show how far the symbol is from flat. Every keystoned render that failed at 6-20 % and 3-6 px/module read when sampled through the geometry it was drawn with, finder centres refined to within a tenth of a module. The parallelogram of the three centres put the bottom-right alignment pattern 17 to 30 modules off at versions 31-40, and the widening search anchored on the pattern one lattice step in. Version 1, with nothing to anchor, was sampled through that parallelogram and missed its far corner by up to 2 modules.

  Along each finder line a plane in perspective changes the module size: the size at one end over the size at the other is the square of the ratio of the two ends' projective weights. So the three centres and the four sizes at the ends of the two lines fix one plane (`FinderFrame`, exact to a hundredth of a module on any plane in `FinderFrameTest`). The frame is refused in favour of the parallelogram when the weights would put the vanishing line across the symbol. zxing-cpp reaches the same corner by intersecting lines fitted to the finders' ring edges, extrapolating seven modules of edge across the symbol. ZXing.Net corrects the parallelogram linearly and searches 4, 8 and 16 modules around it, CodeGlyphX searches one window at whole pixels and then by brute force, and go-qr samples affine only. None of them uses the change of size across the whole line between two finders, which the frame measures.

  Switching each part off alone when it shipped (2026-09-25) measured its worth: the prediction at the frame gave 130 of the sweep's 190 keystone reads gained and half the corpus's 34, the frame as the last grid 47 of the 190, and the timing match through the frame 47 of 400 at 40-50 %. Before the frame, the mesh seeded from the parallelogram had found 0 to 2 of its 16 to 36 nodes in all but two of the failing large renders. The mesh's first-row seeds from the frame changed nothing and were removed.

- A measurement's resolution decides where it may be used. The frame is only as good as the change of size it reads. Whole-pixel runs give sizes in twelfths of a pixel, a median 2 % off and up to 7 % on 400 keystoned renders, which put the frame's prediction up to 8 modules off at versions 31-40. Midpoint crossings of the luminance interpolated along the line give 0.5 % and up to 2 %, 2 modules at worst, well inside the lattice step. Darkness integrated along the line gave 1.3 % and up to 5 % (6.5 modules at worst), because it depends on the levels' calibration, while a crossing depends only on their midpoint. The centre refinement keeps its runs: sub-pixel sizes there too moved flat renders (anti-aliased at 1.0-1.25 px/module +49 −6), a lead for low density rather than keystone.

  So grey images measure crossings. A binarized image, whose edges are always whole pixels, uses the change its runs show only when it exceeds their resolution (more than four twelfths of a pixel between the two ends). Unbounded, two flat binarized renders at 2.6-2.8 px/module that had read before failed, among 4,000. A bound of two thirds of a pixel cost about 50 binarized keystone reads, and a bound of exactly a third let float rounding decide on the twelfths lattice (2 losses in 4,000 renders against none). Weighing a binarized image's runs at all is its whole keystone gain (323 of 4,000 when they shipped).

  The two ends of a line are compared at one resolution: when either end's crossing walk does not finish, both sizes on that line come from runs, and the other line keeps its crossings. The frame predicts where to look but samples only as the last grid. Used first where nothing anchors the corner, it lost flat anti-aliased renders at 1.25-1.3 px/module, where sizes 1-2 % off read as perspective.

- The stages in front of the frame, not the frame, were the limit. With true sizes the frame predicts the alignment pattern within 0.15 module at every version, and at 40-50 % keystone, given the true dimension, the anchored grid of every render whose finders were right lay within 0.16 module of the drawn one. When the frame shipped, every render still failing at 20-30 % keystone and 3-6 px/module either had no three finders found or had a false candidate in the chosen triple, and each read through its true geometry. At 40-50 %, five more had the drawn finders and the wrong dimension. The stages were then counted one at a time (the full sweep's candidates against the drawn finders, the triple chosen, the dimension, and the grid at the true dimension), and each repair went to the stage the counts pointed to: the column's window, the rising diagonal, the dimension from each line, the alternative triples and the corner from the timing patterns, above.

- A third finder inferred from two is a search, not a construction. The construction (the perpendicular of a pair's edge, or half of it from the diagonal's midpoint) is exact on a flat symbol and 1.5 to 1.9 modules out on the glare photographs, past the 0.75 the centre refinement reaches. The probe that settled the design (2026-10-11) decoded each photograph with two finders among the candidates three ways: from the true third centre, 11 of 12 read; from the construction, 6; from the centre searched on the timing patterns to two modules out, 10. The search is what ships, with the rule that on a tie the centre nearer the construction wins, because the exact construction of a flat symbol was wandering off its own centre to another position reading no module wrong.
- A model wrong in one way is not repaired by a parameter for another. The lines through the inferred finder are taken flat, since its end cannot be measured, and that was expected to bound the keystone; a size ratio for those lines, searched together with the position, moved neither the envelope (0.20 keystone before and after, version 3 at 6 px/module) nor the corner reported, and was removed. A ratio at a fixed position never improved the timing share either: the two are coupled, and the best position at one ratio is not the best at another.
- A stage that reads more moves the premises of other tests. Three of the uneven-lighting ramps, pinned to the regional pass, now read at the global threshold: the threshold loses the dark corner's finder and keeps the other two, which is the inference's case. They are listed with the cases the global threshold reads, and the shadows still pin the regional pass.
- A cue that holds on the photographs can fail on the render built to test it. On the two `lots` photographs the symbol's own triples were the most compact of the well-shaped ones (ranks 0 to 5 of 291), so a compactness tie rule in the selection read them; on a keystoned grid of nine the most compact well-shaped triple is the crossroads of three symbols, eleven modules a leg against a symbol's fourteen, and under 0.15 keystone the own triples score outside the tie band altogether. The tie rule was removed before it was measured on a set, and the cue kept only as an order of the triples the timing patterns gate, where a wrong order costs a gate and not a read.
- A grid at the edge of its correction is decided by where its fourth point sits within a tenth of a module. On the four curved version 1 photographs the finder centres are within a fifth of a module of the truth and the symbol reads with 4 or 5 corrections through the true fourth point, so the parallelogram's point, a module out, was the whole gap; a probe that moved the true point a tenth of a module read 2 to 8 of 8 directions. The point measured from the finders' edges lands within a fifth, and one pass or level of each photograph reads. The renderer that reproduces this is the camera's cylinder seen at a tilt about the columns' axis, not the bowed renderer's sine, on which an edge followed over seven modules extrapolates 0.5 to 3 modules out.
- Where a strided triple failed, the question is whether the stride could have confirmed it at all. The five 12-megapixel scenes of 3 to 4.5 px/module symbols were selected from three to six candidates seen on a row or none, with the real triple in the full sweep's list in every one, and four read from that list's own selection; what cost a full sweep on every failing image before (3.1 to 6.2 ms on 740 px noise) costs it only on lists the stride cannot have confirmed, which noise at 740 px (stride 3, a 2 px band) never is.

- Reading every symbol of an image is the one-symbol search repeated, and three things that search could leave alone decide how many it reads (2026-10-14, BoofCV's photographs). The passes have to go on after a read: of the 202 later reads on photographs of two to four codes, 30 came from a pass the first read had ended. A pass has to get past what it cannot read: the stages read 32 candidates and then give the pass up, so the finders of eleven symbols that do not read there hide every symbol scanned after them. And a pass that gave up has to be asked again once another pass has read what stood in its way. With the passes going on and nothing else the entry read 1,038 codes, with a head of the list leaving it once the stages give up on it 1,061, and with a second round 1,071, the count of painting each read symbol over and calling again. A second round whenever the first read anything costs 4.4 times the one-symbol call over the set. Asking first whether a later read changed a list that was given up on costs 2.5, and two rounds read all that four do.
- A sheet of 60 codes does not fit the one-symbol search's candidate list. That list holds 32 candidates, ten symbols' finders, and the scan fills it from the top of the image. The entry that returns every symbol scans into a list of 256, doubled when a scan fills it, and hands the stages its first 32, which are the candidates the one-symbol search holds (`FinderKeptListParityTest`). In a scratch build with the search's own list at 256, the seven 60-code photographs put 151 to 182 candidates in it.

### Piecewise mesh (version 7+)

- The piecewise mesh must not trust any single upstream estimate. Every naive seeding strategy failed measurably before the shipped design was found:

  - (a) Predicting all lattice nodes through the global transform fails when the mesh is needed, because its fourth anchor has the parallelogram error (≈ 2·keystone-shrink, ~9 modules at v20/4%).
  - (b) A finder-only affine seed drifts up to ~1.5 modules mid-edge, because projective foreshortening makes lattice spacing non-uniform.
  - (c) Linear extrapolation of the prediction-only edge nodes fails for the same reason: lattice points are collinear, but their spacing along the line is projective (measured 12 px off where quadratic Lagrange left 1 px).
  - (d) Wide search windows turn data-area false positives into cascading mesh corruption, because the wavefront passes every accepted node on into later predictions.

  The design shipped then combined wavefront parallelogram prediction from processed neighbors, tight (2.5-module) windows with a wider window only for starters, iterated homography refinement anchored on the farthest detected node, and the single transform, always tried as well, so the mesh never reads less than that transform. Since 2026-10-12 each node is predicted by the finders' frame and the offsets of the nodes beside it, and searched within four modules of that (below).

- A plane in perspective is one projective map, so an anchored transform reads every flat symbol the mesh reads. Over the keystone envelope (versions 14 to 40, 20 payloads a version, 540 renders a cell), the sweep (54,400 renders) and the real images, no read changed with the mesh switched off. Inside the envelope the mesh read 3,647 of 6,480 renders, and the anchored transform read each of them at the same attempt with corners as close or closer. In most cells at 3 to 6 px/module it needed no corrections, where the mesh needed up to 696.
- The mesh is needed where no one transform fits. With the bottom-right alignment pattern painted over, only the mesh read 398 of those 6,480 renders (401 with only its centre module flipped), and on the renders it read, its corners were a median 0.01 to 0.13 module off per cell, against 0.32 to 0.50 through the grid that reads without it (0.57 against 2.02 at worst). On a symbol bowed off the plane, its rows sagging 1 to 4 modules at the middle (versions 14 to 40, 2.2 to 5 px/module, 525 renders), nothing else read any of the 519 that read. At a sag of 0.5 to 0.75 module, nothing else read 101 of 210. A painted-over pattern can still anchor the transform on another mark: 70 of 525 such renders read only through the mesh after it.
- So the anchor decides the order. The mesh comes first only when the alignment search found nothing. Otherwise it runs after the anchored transform and its coverage re-read. Every read stayed the same on every set above. Over the 9,720 intact envelope renders the mesh grid was decoded 12 times instead of 4,515, and a sample of them decoded in 0.88 of the time. End to end, the benchmark's version 25 in perspective and turned version 40 took 0.89 to 0.93, its blurred and fractional version 40 0.96 to 0.98, and the rest 1.00. Lost-alignment renders took 1.01. Putting the mesh after the transform unconditionally also keeps the reads, but then a nearly flat symbol with its pattern lost reads through the parallelogram first, its far corner past half a module on 104 of 525 renders, and lost-alignment decodes took 1.13. This was measured on 2026-09-27 by switching grids off in a probe build.

- Versions 7 to 13 bend too, and their lattice is too small for the large one's rules. Bowed as the tests draw it (rows sagging 0.5 to 3 modules at the middle), versions 14-20 read 640 of 700 through their mesh, while versions 7-13, with no mesh, read 191 of 1,400, all with sags under 1.5 modules. zxing-cpp read 1,393. A 3 × 3 lattice has two interior nodes per line, too few to extrapolate an edge line through, and four nodes give a wavefront nothing to pass on. So each interior node was searched where the finders' frame put it, and the plane that best fitted the three finder centres and the found nodes placed the rest (the coordinate-6 row and column, and any interior node not found), until the one builder of 2026-10-12 measured those too (below). The mesh is kept when half the searched nodes are found, and it runs where the large one does.

  Versions 7-13 now read 551 and 561 of 1,400 on two seeds, binarized ones 118 → 512, and the photograph `qrcode-3/22` reads at every right angle. A version 10 whose bottom-right alignment pattern is painted over, which had fallen back to the parallelogram, reads through the mesh with its far corner 0.07 module off. Nothing was lost on the sweep (54,400), the envelope (24,000), the corpus or these sets.

  Each node was searched in a tight window first, then a wider one, until 2026-10-12 (one window of four modules since, below). The tight window alone misses the nodes a 3.5-module sag moves out of it (545 of the 551). The wide window alone reads fewer dots drawn off their module centres (777 of the 783 in 900, and on one it finds none of the four nodes the tight window finds) and fewer binarized bows (509 of 512). The dotted symbol of `SmallLatticeMeshDecodeTest` read under nudges of ±0.05 px/module, ±0.5° and ±0.02 module of shift, and with the wider window alone it failed at 8 of those 9. The remaining failures are bows past 1.5 modules, 26 of 841: the plane puts the edge nodes flat where the arc is steepest, while the larger lattices extrapolate them along it. Placed after the parallelogram when nothing anchored, the small mesh read the same, which is why it runs where the large one does. Below version 7 there is no mesh, and bowed versions 2 to 6 read 196 of 700.

  It slowed failures. Failing damaged versions 7 to 13 took 2 to 6 % longer, and because it also runs when a wrong dimension of 45 to 69 is retried, two failing photographs (`qrcode-3/03`, `high-res-1`) took about 10 % longer. An anchor found by correlating the 5 × 5 pattern around the frame's prediction read 2 of 7 photograph turns tried, so it is not a lever (measured 2026-09-28).

- A curled large symbol fails at its edge, so the edge is where to measure. The corpus's `high-res-1` is a version 34 on curled paper at 2.2 px/module, and its mesh keeps 13 to 24 of 25 nodes. At 0° the interior cells read no function module wrong, while the bands along the extrapolated coordinate-6 row and column read about half of theirs wrong. Only the version read beside a finder names version 34: the decoder samples 145 and 149 and drops the version the 149 grid names, and 153 fails too. The lead there is the dimension from that finder-local read; the edge nodes are measured since 2026-10-11 (below), which did not read it, and the version read at the finders since 2026-10-12, which reads it at 0° and 180°.
- The coordinate-6 nodes are measured, not extrapolated, since 2026-10-11. On BoofCV's `high_version/image020`, a version 30 on bent paper at 7.9 px/module whose 25 interior nodes are all found, the extrapolation along each lattice line, from three nodes a cell apart over a cell and more, carries the found nodes' noise several times over: the mesh read with 271 corrections and its outer bands sampled 45 to 50 % of their modules wrong against 7 to 15 % in the interior. The edge nodes between the corners are alignment patterns like the interior ones, on the timing lines, and the search that finds the interior ones finds every one of them within a module of the extrapolation, in a window of 2.5 modules, with no false hit on the timing modules (the row scan's light-dark-light runs are everywhere on a timing line, and the column cross-check and both rings refuse them). With them measured and the three corners interpolated from each finder's centre and two found nodes a cell in (the local affine of three measured points, exact in perspective over the three modules and following a bend), the mesh reads with 20 corrections and the bands sample 0 to 17 % wrong. Two other corner rules were tried and refuted on the way: the finders' frame's own axes at each finder place the corner within 0.1 module where the frame is measured and 0.6 out on a 0.15 keystone render, and the plane that best fits the three finder centres and every node found puts the corners a module out on the bent photograph (bands 38 to 53 %) and breaks the bowed renders, whose columns are straight and whose extrapolation is exact: no one plane fits a bend, a local measurement does. The lattice is not symmetric about the symbol's centre (the first gap, 6 to the second coordinate, is shorter than the others), so the corner is not on the diagonal from its finder's centre to the diagonal node, which the first interpolation assumed and the top-right band showed, 52 % wrong. On the sweep the measured edge nodes read 72 more camera renders (barrel distortion 47 to 71, bowed 390 to 394, the phone mix 191 to 235) at no cost on what read (1.00 in sum, worst 1.12; noise 1.00, a ramp 0.98). Since 2026-10-12 the corners come from each finder's outline and every node is searched within four modules of its prediction (below): this is the record of the builder that one replaced.
- A lens moves the lattice off every plane, and by little from one node to the next, so since 2026-10-12 the mesh predicts how far a node is off the finders' frame, not where it is. A probe drew the 137 renders of the phone mix and the barrel kind that zxing-cpp read and this library did not, and measured each stage against where the camera drew every module. 132 read with the lens term taken out, the finders were right on 136, and the grid at the drawn positions read all 137. From version 14 the mesh had found 829 of 1,685 interior nodes: its first node came from the finders' parallelogram, up to 5.6 modules out, and every later one from that; the same node from its drawn neighbours is 0.1 to 1.6 out. The pattern search was not at fault: from the drawn position it found 1,505 of 1,669 patterns with the finders' axes and all of them with the local ones. The frame carries the perspective, the neighbours' offsets carry what the frame cannot hold, and the window only has to cover what changes between two nodes: on those renders the rebuilt mesh finds every pattern on a timing line and all but 3 of 1,905 inside. A window of 2.5 modules ahead of the wide one, which the first mesh needed because a wide window let a wrong node into every later prediction, now reads one photograph fewer and no render more: the prediction was what had been wrong, not the window.
- What stands nearest the finders is measured first. The patterns on the timing lines and the corner nodes were the last placed and the least exact, extrapolated from the interior or placed by a plane. Searched first and outward from the finders, each with the offset of the node before it, the timing lines' patterns are all found, and the interior follows from them. Without that carried offset 83 barrel renders and 9 of the phone mix are lost. The corner nodes have no pattern, and three rules were measured for them: on the frame, 296 of the phone mix's 340 in the prototype; with their two neighbours' offsets in proportion, 334; from each finder's own outline, 339. In the decoder the outline took the barrel kind from 208 to 220, and measured first, so that the corners' offsets feed the timing lines, to 264.
- Straight cells are neither a lens nor perspective. Through the drawn nodes two nodes a side read 43 of the 55 gap renders at versions 7 to 13 and three a side all 55; through the measured ones, 320 of 340 phone-mix renders against 339, and 263 of 340 at tilt 35 to 55° against 340. A 3 × 3 lattice is then one curved cell over the whole symbol, and the one builder serves every version from 7: the wavefront, the refinement rounds, the edge extrapolation and the fitted plane of the two earlier builders are gone.
- The symbol states its version where a lens does not hide it. Every way the dimension was found ran along lines a lens bends or used sizes it shrinks: on the barrel renders from version 7 the estimate, the count and the match named the drawn dimension on 3 of 340. The two copies of the version information stand within seven modules of a finder, and that finder's measured outline is a frame for them at any dimension: 338 of 340, one wrong. The corpus's `high-res-1`, whose lesson of 2026-10-11 named this lead, reads at two turns.
- A simplification the tests allow is measured on the sets before it is taken. Seven planted faults survived the first round, four of them a piece of the stage that could be taken out. Taken out together they lost 83 barrel renders, 9 of the phone mix and two corpus reads. One at a time, one was the whole loss (the offset carried along the timing lines), one cost a photograph (the corner outline's second measurement), one gained a photograph (the tight window ahead of the wide one) and one changed nothing (the version outline's second measurement). The two that lost nothing were taken out, and the one the renders need got test shots that fail without it.

### Matrix and format decoding

- A placement rule the code lacks cannot be cited as a precedent. The FNC1 placement rule was planned "as a misplaced Structured Append header is", and the Structured Append header is read wherever it sits, with two tests pinning that. FNC1 is the decoder's first placement rule, kept for its own reason.
- A writer's output is not evidence of a reading rule. Two of the three FNC1 writers return a different text for some input (one never doubles a literal `%`, one writes the separator pairs into one segment), and the readers agree on what those symbols say. The `%` rule was pinned on reader behaviour and on zxing-cpp's unit test vectors, and the fixtures of those symbols carry the reader's text with the writer's input beside it ([qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md)).
- A mirrored matrix does not reliably fail at the format stage. The transposed format bit sequence can land within BCH correction distance of a different valid format pattern, so a mirrored image can surface as `DataUncorrectable` (the wrong mask garbles everything downstream) instead of `FormatInformationInvalid`. The mirror retry (transpose + re-decode) must therefore trigger on any failure, not just format errors.
- Testing "corrupted format info" needs care for the same reason. Flipping all 15 format bits gives the complement, which may be close to another valid codeword, so the negative test searches for a pattern with distance > 3 from all 32 candidates instead of assuming any corruption is rejected.
- A rule enforced by one conditional needs a test that fails without it. The Structured Append header is attached only on `Success` and needs 16 bits after its mode indicator. Deleting the first conditional, or loosening the guard to 15 bits, left the whole suite green: the stream tests called the bit-stream decoder directly, every fixture decoded, and the seeded fuzz test reached the header only with a multiple of four bits left. Every matrix fixture is now also decoded into a one-character destination and must come back without the header, and four hand-built streams sit at 15 to 18 remaining bits. A fixed seed covers only the branches it happens to reach, so boundaries are written by hand.
- The RS decoder's convention must be read off the encoder, not assumed. QR uses generator roots α^0..α^(n-1) (b = 0), which puts an X_k factor in the Forney formula that b = 1 conventions omit. Deriving it from `EccBinaryEncoder`'s documented generator polynomial made the round trip pass on the first run.

### Performance

End-to-end numbers are in `src/FeatherQR.Benchmark`. `QRCodeDecodeEndToEnd` covers the matrix (scenarios mirroring the encode ones), correctable damage and a version 6 image. `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` covers large and no-symbol images, with a fractional pitch, a rotation and a soft render beside the hard ones, because a shape at a whole number of pixels per module measures an alignment as much as a stage. Every change to the shared threshold and finder scan is also measured on the Micro QR and rMQR image classes.

- Codeword extraction was 78 % of a large matrix decode, and the benchmark had misattributed it. A stage profile of `TryDecode(QRCodeData)` at versions 39 and 40 (x64, 2026-09-20) gave extraction 115 to 140 µs of 150 to 178, the bit stream reader 28 to 36, and everything else under 5 %. The per-module walk paid a blocked-bit test, a stream-end test, a data-dependent branch and a memory OR per module (3.8 ns a module at mask 0), and the mask predicate on top made the cost depend on the mask: 114 µs at mask 0, 147 to 154 at masks 5 to 7. `QRCodeStructuredAppendDecode` showed that as a 1.26x "header cost", because its two arms re-encode the content and are free to pick different masks. Two arms are comparable only when the stage under them does not depend on something they choose differently. With the run walk the ratio is 1.00 on every shape. End to end, a version 40 symbol went 170 → 43 µs, and version 10 15 → 4.4 µs.
- Two expected wins in that kernel measured nothing, and one expected loss was real. Replacing the per-run division with a reciprocal multiply was inside the noise, so the division stayed. The bounds-checked form of the walk measured about 28 % slower, so the unchecked one shipped behind two entry checks (mask pattern in range, matrix at least size²). The unpack in front of it (`QRCodeData.GetCoreData`, 3.8 µs) looked like a stage worth designing around, until it turned out to be one call away from the encoder's vector bit expansion, which writes the same layout in 0.4 µs. Check whether a stage is slow or just unoptimized before removing it.
- The bit stream reader took one bit per call, and after the extraction change it was two thirds of a large decode. `BitReader.Reads` looped over a bounds-checked single-bit read, about 1.2 ns a bit. It now takes a field out of a 64-bit window (one big-endian load, two shifts. The last seven bytes of a stream are assembled bytewise). A Byte segment is read in one call, a copy when the payload is byte aligned and a shift of eight bytes a step otherwise. On net8.0 and later the Byte segment's text is one pass of the framework's transcoder, which checks validity as it writes, replacing a hand-written validator followed by a count and a transcode. The version 40 bit stream stage on x64 went Byte 27.8 → 0.1 µs, UTF-8 behind an ECI 28.4 → 1.8, mixed 36.2 → 2.0, Numeric 31.3 → 7.0, and end to end 43 → 15 to 22 µs a symbol (4.4 → 1.7 at version 10). The reader is shared, so Micro QR and rMQR decode through it too. A failed read now throws before it consumes anything, where the bit loop first consumed what was left.
- One transcoder pass has to answer "too small" before it knows whether the text is valid. Undeclared bytes are UTF-8 only if every sequence is well formed, and ISO-8859-1 otherwise, and a one-pass transcoder meets a short destination before it has seen the rest. Reporting `DestinationTooSmall` is safe either way: UTF-16 units never outnumber UTF-8 bytes, substitutions included, so a destination too small for the UTF-8 reading is too small for the char-per-byte one. The same fact makes the explicit return an equivalent mutant of falling through to the ISO-8859-1 size check. It stays so a reader need not know the inequality to see that UTF-8 text is never widened. The Shift_JIS guess narrowed it: a Shift_JIS reading needs a character a pair, fewer than its bytes, so the early answer is given only for a segment that is valid UTF-8 or that the guess rules out, and a guessed segment is counted by its own reading. The strict validator stays for the older targets and for the Micro QR generator's mirror of this rule. `ByteSegmentCharsetParityTest` checks both implementations and the mirror against an oracle that uses neither.
- Two loop rewrites of the numeric and alphanumeric payloads measured nothing or worse, and a third was not worth its path. Keeping the output index in a local and dropping the per-group bit check (the payload check above the loop already covers it) left Numeric at 7.0 µs and slowed the mixed shape from 2.0 to 3.7 µs, because a slice per segment costs more on a plan's short runs than the local saves on a long one. Five 10-bit groups per window load were estimated at 7 → 4.8 µs, about 10 % of a pure-numeric version 40 decode, at the price of a second decode path and a peek API in the shared decoder, and were deferred. After this phase extraction is the largest stage again (about 11 of 15 µs on Byte).
- With the mask and the reader fixed, the Structured Append ratio shows alignment. A version 10+ set symbol's header (20 + 4 + 16 bits) leaves its Byte payload byte aligned and the plain symbol's (4 + 16) does not, so the set takes 0.94 of the plain symbol's time. Behind a 12-bit ECI header it is the other way round, 1.05. Both are the copy against the shift in `ReadBytes`, under 1 µs.
- Damage on a large symbol shows end to end only when it reaches most blocks. A clean symbol exits after its syndromes, so `QR_*_Corrected_Decode` flips modules and keeps a draw only when the decoder reports exactly that many corrected errors, because a flip on a function pattern carries no codeword. Version 1-L with 2 errors went 302 → 526 ns. Version 40-H with 6 errors measured the same as clean (21.65 and 21.63 µs), since at least 75 of its 81 blocks stayed clean and the corrections were inside the run-to-run noise. With 81 errors, about one a block, it went 21.66 → 38.68 µs (x64, 2026-10-02).
- For a large symbol the image path is 25x the matrix decode, and its largest stage is the histogram. The same x64 measurement (2026-09-21, hard-edged synthetic renders at 3, 4 and 8 px/module, one decode attempt) gave Otsu 120 to 220 µs, finder search 65 to 150, dimension estimate plus mesh plus sampling 120 to 180, and matrix decode 14.5. The Otsu figure does not rise steadily with the pixel count (184 µs for 555² against 122 for 740²), because the fill's uniform-group fold needs eight equal pixels in a row, which 3 px/module almost never gives. So the most common module sizes take the per-pixel path, on the two-valued input that path handles worst. That lead shipped. See the histogram entry below.
- A short kernel can finish measuring before the JIT has promoted it. With warmup by iteration count, the first shape of a process measured 2x to 8x slow for the fast kernels but correctly for the 100 µs reference. Warming up by time removed the error.

- The syndrome pass dominates steady-state cost. Every decode pays it (clean blocks exit early after it), and Berlekamp-Massey/Chien/Forney run only on blocks that contain errors. A GFNI kernel (net10.0+ x64, `EccBinaryDecoder.X86.cs`) measured ~284× per version-40 block, and end-to-end version-40 matrix decode dropped 369 µs → 131 µs, so decode is now faster than encode. An AdvSimd kernel (net8.0+ ARM64, `EccBinaryDecoder.Arm64.cs`, 2026-08-20) closes the same gap on ARM: 11-61× the scalar log-domain kernel as a four-byte step, 61× per version-40 block, and Standard QR v1 matrix decode 1,586 → 1,103 ns on Apple M2.

  The ARM kernel is not a port of the GFNI design. GF2P8MULB is hardwired to the AES polynomial, so the x64 design is built around a field isomorphism that lets it borrow that instruction. PMULL has no fixed modulus, so ARM pays for the reduction mod 0x11D (by nibble-split table lookup) and reads the per-byte data terms from 24 KB of lazily built tables. A 3 KB nibble-split alternative to those tables was measured and lost by 20-78 %, a verdict from a core with a 128 KB L1D, which is also why the scalar fallback is kept fast. The reduction tables are hoisted into locals: the JIT does not CSE `Vector128.Create` over a static array across the loop body, so left inline every reduction pays two extra loads, worth up to 20 % of the kernel. The same round improved the scalar tier, which netstandard2.0/2.1 runs, to four syndromes per pass (2.2-2.9× on large blocks). That tier keeps the Horner multiply in log domain: the multiplier's log is the constant i, so a step is one zero-check, one log load and one exp load, measured 0.84-0.90x of the `GaloisField.Multiply` form.

  Every build without the 256-bit GFNI tier runs a 128-bit kernel (`EccBinaryDecoder.Vector128.cs`, 2026-10-01): x64 without AVX, x64 on a CPU without GFNI, .NET 8 on x64 (GFNI is a .NET 10 API, so .NET 8 ran the scalar pass even with AVX2), and WebAssembly. It is the AdvSimd kernel's structure on portable vectors, and does the multiply that `PMULL` does, by each lane's constant K (a fixed power of α), through linearity. a·K is the XOR of K·x^b over the set bits b of a, so a multiply is eight rounds of a sign-bit mask, an AND with a plane of K·x^b and an XOR, from 768 bytes of planes and with no reduction. It runs the pass in 0.06 to 0.18 of the scalar time on a default NativeAOT publish, 0.06 to 0.23 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.14 to 0.36 interpreted (148-, 45- and 24-byte blocks).
