Version 40 matrix decode takes 0.21, 0.25 to 0.32 and 0.33 of its time before. Berlekamp-Massey/Chien/Forney stay scalar on every target.

- The ARM syndrome kernel was bound by its carried chain, and the fix was re-association, not a split. With a four-byte Horner step, the AdvSimd kernel's chain (acc → PMULL → UZP → TBL → EOR, about 14 cycles a step on Apple M2) was the whole cost: Reed-Solomon took 5.4 µs of a 19.6 µs version 40 decode there, against 1.7 of 15 on x64 behind GFNI, and halving the vector work had gained only 20 %. An earlier attempt, never shipped, split the accumulator chain four ways across the codeword. It measured −21.5 % at 149 codewords but lost at rMQR sizes (no rMQR block exceeds 68 codewords), because a split's combine multiplier depends on the block length and its fixed cost does not shrink with the block.

  Re-associating Horner instead takes eight bytes a step: the multiply that joins two four-byte data terms depends on data alone, so it falls off the chain. This form has no length-dependent term and won at every block shape the three symbologies use, measured through `TryCorrect` on the M2 (2026-09-21):

  - 0.53x to 0.54x at version 40's 145- to 153-byte blocks.
  - 0.75x to 0.83x over rMQR's 25- to 68-byte blocks (54 shapes, 0.45x to 0.98x).
  - 0.76x to 0.81x at Micro QR M3 and M4, level at M2, and 1.07x (5 ns) at M1's five-byte block.
  - On the syndrome pass alone, 0.44x at 148 bytes and 0.59x at 45.

  The sixteen-byte tree tied at 148 and lost 10 % at 45, because from eight bytes on the loop is throughput-bound (about 100 instructions a step). Two throughput hypotheses were refuted in the same round (immediate-offset row pairing lost 10 %, pre-split multiplier halves tied), and work on the loop stopped there. Version 40 Byte matrix decode went 19.5 → 16.7 µs on the `QRCodeData` entry and 19.1 → 16.2 on the span entry. Version 10 went 2.07 → 1.84 and version 1 0.28 → 0.26. The kernel is still shared by all three symbologies.

- A flat ns-per-iteration across sizes means one kernel is the whole cost. Before the AdvSimd tier, ARM matrix decode ran at a constant 3.07-3.15 ns per syndrome inner-loop iteration across a 50x size range, which proved the syndrome pass was nearly all of it. The same item was already under 1 % on x64 after GFNI, so ARM was still at the pre-GFNI position. Re-run that ratio before assuming a component still dominates.
- The syndrome destination is 32 bytes wide, not `eccCount`. Every vector tier keeps every syndrome in lanes and stores whole registers, so `ComputeSyndromes` requires an `EccBinaryDecoder.SyndromeLanes`-length span regardless of the ECC count, and lanes past `eccCount` hold meaningless syndromes of unused roots. This is a caller contract across symbologies. A caller sizing the span to `eccCount` throws on x64 (the GFNI store is bounds-checked) but silently corrupts memory on ARM64, so x64 CI cannot catch the ARM failure mode. Each kernel has a test of its own store width (`GfniKernel_WritesExactlySyndromeLanes`, `AdvSimdKernel_WritesExactlySyndromeLanes`, `Vector128Kernel_WritesExactlySyndromeLanes`).
- The isomorphism root matters. β = 0x03 makes φ its own inverse, so one matrix constant serves both directions. The ×4 unroll measured 29 % over unroll ×2 and 47 % over the plain recurrence. Unrolling beyond ×4 stalls, because the loop moves from latency-bound (accumulator chain) to bound by GFNI-port throughput. Pre-mapping the whole codeword to remove the in-loop affine measured slower: that affine was off the carried dependency chain, so removing it saved nothing, while the extra pass cost real time.
- The large symbols had stopped using the sampler that was vectorized for them. Version 14 and up then sampled through the piecewise mesh first, and that loop had stayed scalar: a cell walk, a division, two lerps and a scattered load per module, 94 to 137 µs at version 40, half of a clean 3 px image decode once the threshold was fast. It became cheap through where things are computed, not only through vector width. The cell a column falls in and the fraction across it are the same for every row, so they go in a table once a call and the division leaves the module loop (0.78 on its own. This step is portable, and it is what the netstandard builds run. Every .NET build class has had a vector tier since, below). A cell's start and span are taken once a row, and an 8-module vector step is built from them by broadcast. Only the steps that straddle two cells need a select, and the version alone decides which those are. Version 40 sampling went 114 → 19 µs, version 20 33 → 6.3, and 135 → 28 on a 3.5 MB rotated image where the loads were expected to be the limit. It is now cheaper than the global transform's vector rows on the same grid, which cannot hoist their division out of the loop.
- A sampler is right only when it picks the same pixel, and three things decided that. The multiply and the add stay separate, because fused they can differ by an ulp and truncate into the next pixel. The float-to-int conversion has to match the reference's, whose cast differed by runtime: before .NET 9 it was the raw x64 conversion (INT_MIN for NaN and for anything out of range, 0 after the clamp), from .NET 9 it saturates, and on WebAssembly it differs again between interpreted and AOT-compiled code. The tier at first had a form for each .NET, found only because the parity test runs on net8.0 as well as net10.0. The kernel search had run on one. Since the 128-bit tier (2026-09-30), the reference takes each coordinate through `PixelIndex.Clamp`, which clamps to the far edge before the conversion and gives the same pixel on every runtime, and every tier has one form. The upper clamp is a float minimum with the limit as the first operand, so a NaN lane passes through, converts to INT_MIN and becomes 0 at the integer maximum, where the reference puts it. The other operand order turns NaN into the far edge of the image. None of these show on a symbol inside its image with finite nodes, so the test scenes are built from what can go wrong: every mesh version, bent meshes, nodes off their predictions, symbols pushed past all four image edges, and nodes that are NaN, infinite or past int range.
- Several variants were refuted on the way, each for a reason worth keeping.
  - Spreading a start and a span to all 177 columns every row, to get the cell index out of the loop, cost more in stores than the indirection it removed (77 → 102 µs). The first vector form built on it measured 0.72 and nearly closed the question, because a variant whose parent was refuted also measures the parent's cost.
  - Branchless clamps gained nothing, since a symbol inside its image never takes those branches.
  - An AVX2 gather lost 9 % to eight scalar loads, and would have read past the last pixel.
  - Removing a register spill by interleaving the per-cell arrays lost 5 to 10 %: a spill that is one load is not worth a more expensive address.
  - Two mutants survived the first planted-fault run, and both were the tests' fault: a y clamp against the x limit (every test image was square), and `<` for `<=` on the threshold (every pixel was 0 or 255). The scenes are now non-square, with pixels on either side of the threshold.
- Perspective sampling SIMD helps only large symbols. An AVX2 kernel (net8.0+) achieved 2.7× at version 40 (79 µs → 29 µs), with a scalar row-hoisted fallback elsewhere. The loop is not division-bound: module computations are independent, so out-of-order execution hides division latency (halving the division count measured no gain), and the cost was scalar conversion, clamp and branch overhead. Sampling is ~0.8% of a typical (version 4) image decode, so the win matters for large symbols only. The overhead finding transfers to 128-bit lanes. A Vector128 kernel (two independent 4-lane chains per iteration plus a 4-lane cleanup tail, with exactly the scalar op sequence so lanes stay bit-identical) gave Apple M2 1.84–1.93× across versions 4–40. The two-chain unroll and the cleanup tail are each worth only 2–5%, which confirms fdiv latency is mostly hidden even at 128 bits and the win comes from amortizing fixed per-iteration work. frecpe reciprocal estimate and FMA are excluded by contract, not cost: both break the SIMD-equals-scalar byte identity that keeps the fallback testable.
- Alignment search cost is dominated by the failure path. The expanding window sweep (4→8→16 modules) runs to completion when no pattern exists, up to 4× per failed decode (secondary dimension × inversion), and was a baseline ~40% of an image decode. An AVX2 kernel (32-px SIMD dark-mask classification + tzcnt run walk × a ⌊moduleSize/2⌋ row stride) achieved 23× on the not-found sweep. On that sweep the row stride measured 4×, and the vector classify with the tzcnt run walk 6.4× on x64. The vertical cross-check recenters exactly, so striding gives identical results. The finder scan's walk-vs-build split (below) transfers intact to this kernel's much shorter windows (65–257 px vs full rows): the same NEON 64-px fold + portable 16-px tier gave Apple M2 1.4× at the prediction, 3.8× at 3 modules off and 5.8× on the not-found sweep. The same caveat applies: the walk restructure alone slows the happy path, because a single ~65 px row scan is too short to repay the mask setup without the vector classify. Successful-decode E2E is unmoved (alignment is <1% of `Image_Url_M`). The gain lands on failed decodes of non-QR input.
- Finder scan striding must be envelope-safe, not based on module size. The finder scan reuses the SIMD mask-walk kernel shape, but its row stride cannot come from the module size, which is unknown before detection, so the bound comes from the worst case. The 1:1:3:1:1 band is 3 modules tall for an axis-aligned symbol. (Under rotation the surviving band narrows: the rMQR follow-up measured a floor of 5 rows at 3 px/module, which is why `TryFind` relies on its complementary pass rather than on this arithmetic.) A version-40 symbol filling the frame has the smallest possible modules, so stride 3·height/(4·177) still hits every supported symbol's band several times. A failed stride pass rescans only the skipped rows, keeping its candidates. The union covers exactly the rows of a full scan for one sweep of total work, so detection can never regress (a naive full-rescan fallback measured 0.87×, a regression, in the scalar variant). The best-3 selection before that fallback must run on a copy, because it compacts and sorts the candidate list in place. Together these gave 9.6–11.4× on the scan, and image E2E (`Image_Url_M`) 309 µs → 132 µs (−57%). The SIMD walk alone is bit-identical to the scalar walk and parity-tested.
- The finder scan's SIMD split is walk-vs-build, and only the build is per-ISA. The tzcnt run walk is platform-neutral, and the ~15-line dark-bitmask build is the only ISA-specific piece (AVX2 vpmovmskb / NEON / portable 128-bit `ExtractMostSignificantBits`, gated on `Vector128.IsHardwareAccelerated`, since Vector256 acceleration implies it). NEON has no movemask. Folding 64 pixels into one mask word (4 unsigned compares AND per-byte bit weights + 3 pairwise adds, the simdjson bulk-movemask shape) beat per-16 `ExtractMostSignificantBits` by 8–11% and the scalar walk by 3.3–4.1× on Apple M2. The walk restructure alone (scalar mask build) gave only 1.1–1.4×, so the win comes from the vector classify. Byte-lane `Vector128.LessThan` is already an unsigned compare (cmhi), so the x64 `min(v, t−1) == v` trick is unnecessary on the 128-bit path. Image E2E (`Image_Url_M`, M2) went 129 µs → 76 µs (−41%).

- On a large symbol the finder search is mostly refused cross-checks, and their walk paid for its generality. Once the threshold and the mesh sampler were vector code, the search was 56 to 66 % of a rendered version 40 decode. Such a symbol has 7,800 to 12,200 dark runs on the strided rows, where 280 to 800 windows pass the row's 1:1:3:1:1 check, 6 to 9 % of those pass the column's, and 6 to 21 become candidates. Every other one is a data module, refused after a walk of 30 to 90 pixels that chose its axis per pixel, read each pixel through a checked two-dimensional index, and counted its runs in a stack buffer.

  `FinderPatternFinder.MeasureRuns` is one walk for the column, the row and the diagonal. The distance between two pixels of the line and the pixels on each side of the centre are worked out once, the loops count down, and no reference is formed outside the image. The pixels read, their order and the verdict on the runs are unchanged. The loops it replaced are its reference, run by `TryFindScalar`. `FinderRunWalkParityTest` compares the runs themselves, from every pixel of non-square images, because on most centres the verdict is a refusal whatever the runs were.

  On x64 the finder search took 0.83 to 0.92 of its time on rendered symbols (version 40 at 4 px/module 110 → 97 µs, at 8 px 158 → 140), 0.84 to 0.95 photo-like and 0.89 to 0.99 rotated, and was level on noise, where a walk is 11 pixels long and most windows never reach one. Image decode took 0.83 to 0.95 on rendered symbols, 0.89 to 0.98 photo-like and 0.94 to 1.00 rotated, with the no-symbol inputs level. Fewer than one hit in ten reaches the row or the diagonal walk, so nearly all of that gain is the column's.

- A check that is replaced has to be replaced by evidence as strong, and block noise shows whether it was. A row beside the centre row, read when the centre row fails, takes the finder a hole or a worn ring leaves. From 2 px a module it also let texture through: the row a pixel or two from the scanned row reads whenever the scanned row did, and the check it stood in for was the one that refused. On 540 images of block noise the full sweep's candidates rose from 391 to 483 and the images yielding a triple from 42 to 58. More conditions on the same finder took back under half of it (441 and 53). Both rows, above and below, took back nearly all of it (397 and 43) and lost every photograph the rule gains, whose rings are worn on one side of the centre. A row three pixels off, from 4 px a module, left 421 and 46 with the photographs the same. BoofCV's photographs told the two floors apart by nothing: 456 at either.

- A fallback's cost is what follows it, and counting its events says what to ask first. The row beside the centre row was priced as 1 to 3 % of a clean high-version read and left there. Counted, a version 40 symbol at 3 px a module sent 39 refused centre rows to it, 66 rows walked, 21 of them on to the diagonals, and none became a candidate. What tells a hole from data had been measured and dropped: the refused centre row's five runs and their total. A hole leaves them, and 36 of the 39 had lost them. Asked for them first, the row is walked for 3 (2026-10-13).

- A value read after a refusal has to be the same through the reference. No caller read the total of a refused cross-check, so the bounded walk left it 0 where the reference walk, the one the parity tests compare against, had measured past the bounds and reported it. The row's condition reads it. The reference walk is held to the bounded walk's limits, and the parity test compares the total on a refusal too.

- The prototype promised 0.37 to 0.52 on that walk and the search got about two thirds of it, for the reason the histogram benchmark had already shown. Both arms of the prototype were functions of eight and nine arguments, while the shipped loops had been inline in the cross-check and paid no call, so the copy standing in for them was slower than the code it stood for, and the new walk had to pay for a call the old one never made. As a plain call it was level, to within 2 %, with inlining it into its two callers. The inlined form was ahead on most rows and is the one kept. The same run showed how little one reading is worth here: four passes of one binary on one input spread from 56 to 66 µs, and a gradient with no cross-check at all read 24 against 25.

- A refused cross-check stops walking as soon as it is refused, and the centre run decides that. The false hits on a large symbol are ordinary data: side runs of about two modules around a centre of about three, in a window of about nine. Nothing in them runs long, so tightening the cap on a side run, the original plan, cut the pixels read by 15 %. The accept conditions do give an order:

  - The strict ratio puts three totals below fourteen centres and fourteen side runs below three totals, so a side run is shorter than the centre run.
  - The near-miss ratio ties a side run to a third of the centre.
  - The total is inside its window (within 40 % of the row for the row again, 2/7 to 7/2 of it for the column, see the finder in perspective above) and below fourteen thirds of the centre.

  `FinderPatternFinder.MeasureRunsBounded` therefore measures the centre run first, in both directions. It gives up the walk at the first run that exceeds what is left of those budgets, and an empty side run is a refusal too. A cross section with a centre of one module is refused once its first side run reaches one module. The small crisp runs of the whole-pattern check lie inside the same bounds, so both modes of the axis cross-checks use it. The diagonal has no expected total and walks as before. Pixels read per hit fell to 0.55 to 0.60 on a symbol and 0.67 on noise.

  Exactness is a property of the verdict alone: no run vector outside a bound may be accepted. So `FinderRunBoundsTest` checks `AxisRunBounds` against the ratio checks themselves, over every vector for expected totals up to 40, four hundred thousand more at the tolerance edges up to 400 px/module, and every centre of every total of the window up to 200. The last set is needed because vectors drawn around the nominal shape never land on the corners of the total window, where a bound one step too tight refuses a cross section the verdict accepts. `FinderCrossCheckParityTest` compares the cross-check through both walks bit for bit, grey second look included.

  Both tests were sized against hand-planted faults, every term of the bounds and the walk tightened by one. Ten times as many draws at the tolerance edges caught no fault that 400,000 miss, except three that the exhaustive or the window-corner walk catches, and a second seed of the crisp scenes caught nothing the first misses. Six tightenings survive both tests at their full sizes, and none is a fault the tests miss:

  - Two change no bound (the near-miss floor on the centre is never the lower of the two floors, and the near-miss side cap rounds the same with either constant).
  - One changes only an expected total of 10, which the exhaustive walk covers.
  - Three tighten the like-edge caps where no like-edge cross section reaches them. Summed, the pair and shift conditions keep nineteen side runs at least two below sixteen centres, and three side runs at least two below the total, which every like-edge vector up to twelve modules of 1,200 px bears out.

  Against the unbounded walk (x64, median of six alternating passes), the finder search took 0.91 to 1.01 at version 40 and 3 px/module, 0.81 to 0.86 at 4 px, 0.81 to 0.87 at 8 px, and 0.94 on noise, the first gain of this work on an image with no symbol. With the walk above, against the loops both replaced, it took 0.71 to 0.92 at version 40, image decode 0.78 to 0.98, and no-symbol noise 0.92 to 0.93. A label-sized symbol at 3 and 4 px/module gives a third of the previous gain back (the search 1.03 to 1.06 against the unbounded walk, 0.90 to 0.99 against the old loops), because a fifth of its hits are real finders, walked in full either way, and the bounded walk costs more to enter. Leaving the centre check out did not recover it.

- The row walk was bound by its branches, and a branch-free kernel is worth more inside a decode than on its own. The mask walk judges a window at the end of every dark run with up to fifteen compares, each of which may leave early, and a search judges ten thousand windows on a large symbol and forty-five thousand on an image with no symbol, nearly all refused. With 256-bit vectors or ARM64 AdvSimd, rows of 32 to 4,095 pixels now go to the edge-list kernel (`FinderPatternFinder.RowEdges.cs`). Every 64 pixels become one word, which is never stored, and the word's rising and falling edges fill an array of run starts and one of run ends. Sixteen windows a step (eight on ARM64) are classified without a branch by the same three integer checks (strict ratio, near miss, small crisp runs). Only flagged windows run scalar code, in row order, through the same follow-ups and cross-checks.

  The strict ratio is checked in integers and gives the float form's verdict on every input (they can differ only where total / 7f is inexact, and equality needs a total divisible by 14, where it is exact). Both ratio checks share one difference per run, total − 7·run, written so nothing leaves a sixteen-bit lane, which bounds the row width. Targets with neither instruction set, and wider rows, kept the mask walk. A scalar edge list measured level with it, so the portable tier did not change then (every 128-bit target has taken the kernel since, three entries below). The numbers below are for the x64 tier the kernel was first measured on. ARM64 took the same kernel on 128-bit vectors two entries below.

  The row pass alone on x64 took 0.36 to 0.58 of the mask walk's time on symbols and 0.20 on noise, the ordering unchanged with AVX-512 disabled. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry, against the walks above), version 40 at 3 px/module went 112 → 85 µs, at 3.4 px 127 → 96, rotated 4 px 421 → 276, soft 4 px 298 → 239, the version 6 URL 10.7 → 9.3, no-symbol noise 2,427 → 1,408, and a gradient stayed level. Allocated was unchanged. In the rotated decode the kernel saved three times what it saved on its own (145 µs against 45), because in isolation the old walk's branches are learnt from one row sequence repeated, and in a decode they are not. That is the 1.4× to 1.7× the phase's profile had measured between the two.

- A row kernel that reports a window too many changes no result, so candidate parity cannot test it. The cross-checks judge the same row again with the scalar checks and refuse what the row stage should not have sent. Twelve of twenty-two planted faults in the kernel survived a test that compared candidate lists bit for bit, and every one over-reports or sits in a stage whose output matters only when accepted. So the kernel's two stages became functions of their own. `ExtractRowEdges` is checked against a pixel-by-pixel scan at every length around the vector and word sizes, and `ClassifyWindows` against the scalar predicates themselves, for every run vector up to 14 pixels and three million at the tolerance edges up to the width limit (`FinderRowEdgesTest`). Three faults still survive, all over-reporting by construction: the near-miss flag kept while the grey levels are off, which sends a window the mask walk never measures to the coverage check, and two follow-ups skipped after a flag.

  One class of over-report is visible to candidate parity, and `FinderRowKernelParityTest`'s scene list has the scene that shows it. A finder flush against the right edge, whose ring is light on one row, leaves that row a window short, and because the edge buffer still holds the row above, a lane read past the last window makes a candidate the scalar walk never makes.

- The edge-list kernel also runs on ARM64, built from what that machine makes cheap. After the histogram tier, on the mask walk, the search was 10 to 50 % of a version 40 decode on an Apple M2 and 46 % of a no-symbol noise image. The kernel above now also takes 128-bit vectors:

  - The row's word comes from the NEON fold the mask walk already used (there is no movemask).
  - Eight windows are classified a step (`ClassifyWindows8`. Sixteen as two halves lost 5 to 30 % on the last step of every row).
  - A step's three verdicts become bits (`LaneBits`: narrow, one weight a lane, add across, since `ExtractMostSignificantBits` is a sequence there) only after one add across their OR says a lane is flagged.
  - A word's rising and falling edges are written by one loop, one of each per iteration, so their two two-cycle bit-clear chains overlap (0.78 to 0.92 of two loops in a row on symbols).

  x64 takes the same loop. Its bit clear is one `blsr`, so there is no chain to overlap, and the extraction alone measured level, but the loop branches half as often, and the whole row pass measured 0.85 to 0.97 of two loops on version 40 symbols and level on noise and on a label-sized symbol. End to end that is inside the noise (±3 %), as expected for a few percent of a stage that is a fifth of the decode. It stays because one form on both machines also puts the ARM64 loop under x64 CI. The windows are judged by the same integer arithmetic throughout, and `FinderRowEdgesTest` and `FinderRowKernelParityTest` run on ARM64 unchanged but for the lane count.

  On the M2 the row pass alone took 0.13 to 0.19 of the mask walk's time on rendered version 40 symbols, 0.25 on a label-sized one and 0.37 on noise, where three quarters of what is left is the coverage measurement on near misses, which every kernel pays. In the image decode stage harness, version 40 at 3 px/module went 270 → 138 µs, 3.4 px 300 → 164, 8 px 441 → 302, 4 px rotated 757 → 550, 4 px soft 520 → 326, no-symbol noise 740 × 740 3,377 → 1,778, and a gradient stayed level. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry) the figures were 269 → 137, 307 → 161, 756 → 549, 530 → 334, the version 6 URL 15.4 → 11.6, noise 3,308 → 1,723, Micro QR M4 6.3 → 5.9 and rMQR R17x139 34.5 → 25.1. Allocated was unchanged.

  The kernel's gate also found a separate bug, filed apart: `GreyLevels.FromHistogram` computed the light mean in float, and past 2²⁴ in the weighted sum it rounded above 255 and enabled the grey levels on a two-valued image. The scan bounds are now integers (see the grey-levels entry below).

- Every other 128-bit target also takes the edge-list kernel. x64 without AVX (a default NativeAOT publish) and WebAssembly had kept the mask walk. On them the row's word is four 16-byte compares with a movemask each, and the rest is the ARM64 form: eight windows a step, and the OR of the three verdicts becomes bits first, so a step that flags nothing makes bits once. Against the mask walk (version 40 at 3 px/module and 740 × 740 noise), the row pass alone took 0.43 and 0.54 on default NativeAOT, 0.25 and 0.49 on WebAssembly AOT, and 0.28 and 0.47 interpreted. Image decode took 0.58 to 0.96 on default NativeAOT, 0.36 to 0.80 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.38 to 0.94 interpreted, the gain largest on the version 25 keystone and smallest on the rMQR keystone and the bitmap entries. Those builds never run the test suite, so `--parity` checks the kernel's candidates against the scalar walk's on each of them, and on the JIT with AVX off in CI.

- The mesh sampler had an ARM64 tier, and four lanes gave half of what eight gave. `SampleGridPiecewiseAdvSimd` was the AVX2 tier's step on 128-bit vectors. It ran two steps a loop body and packed their eight pixels into one word for one compare and one store. The tables were read through hoisted references, because a bounds check a step measured 3 to 6 % of the kernel, and the pixel index took one integer multiply-add. The float operations were the same, in the reference's order, so it picked the same pixel. Its clamp had one conversion form where the AVX2 tier needed two, because the scalar cast on ARM64 has always been the saturating fcvtzs. For the same reason its row tail kept the plain cast, where the other tiers' tails use `PixelIndex.Clamp`, which ILC for ARM64 compiled with the limit converted inside the loop. The tier was removed on 2026-10-13: the portable 128-bit tier written after it is the same loop and ran no slower on that machine (the next entry).

  Against the column-table tier on Apple M2 it measured 0.46 to 0.51 at versions 14 to 40, upright and rotated, and the search for a faster form ended there: the loop issues eight to nine instructions a module at about four a cycle. Variants that swapped one instruction for another (cell parameters kept as vectors, pixels loaded straight into lanes) measured level, and an index vector stored and reloaded as words lost 20 % to partial store forwarding. The AVX2 tier reaches 0.24 of the same column-table tier on x64. This ISA has no wider form.

  In the M2 image decode stage harness, version 40 at 3 px/module went 141 → 115 µs, 8 px 293 → 266, 4 px rotated 544 → 521, 4 px soft 325 → 304, and version 20 at 3 px 42 → 34. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry) the figures were 139 → 114, 161 → 137, 545 → 525 and 326 → 303, with the version 6 URL and the no-symbol inputs level. Allocated was unchanged. `SampleGridPiecewiseParityTest` enters the tier where it enters the AVX2 one. Two planted faults survived, and both were examined. One was the minimum's operand order, which `Avx.Min` cares about and `Vector128.Min` does not. The other was in a four-lane leftover loop, since deleted: odd versions leave five modules after the eight-module steps and do enter it, but the scalar tail after it samples the same pixel from the same floats, so no output could tell the two apart.

- Every other 128-bit target also has a mesh tier. x64 without AVX and WebAssembly sampled the mesh through the column table. `SampleGridPiecewiseVector128` is the ARM64 tier's step on portable vectors, taking each coordinate to its pixel through `VectorCast.ToPixel`. On ARM64 itself it was level with that tier: 0.98 to 1.00 of its cycles through three nodes and 0.96 to 1.00 through two, on both JITs of an Apple M2 (2026-10-12). As NativeAOT code, each tier entered directly, it runs 0.98 of the ARM64 tier's instructions and cycles at versions 14, 25 and 40 (2026-10-13), 728 thousand instructions a version 40 sampling against 744, four fewer a pass of eight modules: `VectorCast.ToPixel` converts unsigned (fcvtzu), so no maximum with zero follows, and ILC keeps one more constant in a register. The ARM64 file bought nothing, so it was removed that day and ARM64 takes the 128-bit tier. Through the dispatch the sampler then takes 0.98 on NativeAOT and on the .NET 10 JIT, a bowed version 40 read runs 15 thousand instructions fewer of 11 million, and a read that runs no mesh the instructions it ran. The mesh runs only when nothing anchors the grid or the anchored grid fails. On a bowed symbol it was 9.8 % (version 25) and 11.4 % (version 40) of a WebAssembly AOT decode. Against the column table (version 40 at 3 px), the sampler alone took 0.50 on default NativeAOT, 0.30 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.41 interpreted. Bowed decodes at versions 25 and 40, with the histogram's 128-bit tier, took 0.84 and 0.89, 0.72 and 0.76, and 0.92 and 0.93.
- Three nodes a side cost the sampler a third more than two on x64, and a half to three quarters more on ARM64. In Newton's form a coordinate is start + along × (slope + past × curvature): one more multiply and add an axis than the two-node lerp, two more broadcasts a step and one more column table, with the run of columns that shares its three nodes in place of the cell (a run is 22 modules or more on every lattice, so a step still touches two at most). The AVX2 tier at versions 13, 20, 30 and 40 takes 5.0, 8.2, 16.5 and 26.8 µs against 3.6, 5.9, 11.9 and 20.1 through two nodes, and the column-table tier 10.8, 20.7, 41 and 68 against 9.0, 17.6, 37 and 61 (2026-10-12, one x64 machine, sampling only). The lattice's spacings enter as reciprocals tabled once a call and the reference takes the same reciprocals, so the tiers stay identical to it: the divisions a row were 8 % of the column-table tier and 2 % of the AVX2 one. The ARM64 tier was rewritten by the same edit and run on an Apple M2 the same day. It picks the reference's pixel on the JIT, with `DOTNET_EnableArm64Dp=0`, on a default NativeAOT publish and on one for `armv8-a,-dotprod`, and no multiply and add is fused on either JIT or on ILC, which the parity needs. On .NET 10 it takes 21.0, 34.0, 68.0 and 110.8 thousand cycles a call at versions 13, 20, 30 and 40 against 14.6, 22.4, 41.8 and 71.4 through two nodes (6.6, 10.6, 21.2 and 35.3 µs against 4.3, 6.6, 12.3 and 21.0): 1.44 to 1.63, with 1.59 to 1.78 on .NET 8 and 1.56 at version 40 on NativeAOT. Against the column-table tier it takes 0.43 to 0.52 on .NET 10 and 0.48 to 0.65 on .NET 8, the column table itself costing 1.63 to 1.69 times its two-node form on .NET 10 and 1.28 to 1.30 on .NET 8 and NativeAOT. Part of what ARM64 pays over x64 is in the loop's registers. Its body of eight modules is 156 instructions where it was 114, and thirteen of its values are loaded from the stack frame each pass where four were, eleven table references and two vector constants at two instructions each: 18 of the 42 instructions the third node added (25 loads against 10 on .NET 8). One run of the sampler is about 4 % of a bowed version 40 read, so a tier that held its tables behind fewer references is bounded near 1 % of that read, and none was built.

The report project's reading shapes were timed only when the whole chain was, on an Apple M2 on 2026-10-12: a default NativeAOT publish of each stage's commit, and the instructions a call from the process's own count (`/usr/bin/time -l` over a long loop less a short one), which repeat to four digits where the cycles of two builds running the same instructions moved by up to 5 %.   By piece, in thousands of instructions a decode. The mesh and the version read, each piece run twice so that the read keeps its path: the version read at the finders is 45 to 57 on every shape from version 7, and the whole step where no mesh runs. On the bowed version 25 shape the builder takes 406 where the one it replaced took 227, and the sampler 365 where two nodes took 245; at version 40, 860 for 570 and 744 for 494; the version read 50 on both. The builder at versions 25 and 40 is the three corner outlines, 157 and 144, the patterns on the timing lines, 73 and 175, and the interior, 185 and 560, so at version 40 the interior alone costs what the old builder cost in all. The finder cross-checks, each piece switched off alone: of the 71, 87, 52, 108 and 52 the stage adds on the five unbowed shapes of version 25 and up, the row beside the centre row is 52, 54, 37, 81 and 41, the wider window 5 to 21, the ring without corners under 18 and the crowded list nothing; on the R17x139, 18.5 of 21.2. That row is read when the row again fails and the column's centre run is 12 px or more, which on a clean symbol is a candidate among the data (a finder's own centre is 9 px at 3 px a module), walked along two more rows before it is refused. Since 2026-10-13 the row is read only where the centre row kept five runs of the scanned row's length, and the outlines of the version read are measured only where the symbol does not state the estimate ([Decisions](#decisions)). Counted on x64, the five unbowed shapes walk 5 to 17 such rows a decode where they walked 44 to 87, the R17x139 none for 10, and no shape from version 7 measures the outlines.

Against its ratios the AOT-compiled shapes are at 0.98 to 1.01 and the interpreted ones at 0.97 to 1.04, highest on the bowed version 25 symbol.   The mesh sampler was also timed alone, at version 40 and 3 px a module, because its third node had been timed on x64 and ARM64 only. Through three nodes the 128-bit tier takes 1.46 times its two-node time AOT-compiled (55 µs against 38) and 1.59 interpreted (327 against 206). On default NativeAOT it takes 1.34 (42 against 31), and the JIT's AVX2 tier takes 1.42 (28 against 19). It still beats the column table on both WebAssembly builds, at 0.34 of its time AOT-compiled and 0.45 interpreted, where two nodes took 0.30 and 0.38. What the interpreter pays over NativeAOT's ratio is 51 µs a run of the sampler, about 1 % of an interpreted bowed version 40 read (5.3 ms), so no other form was tried.

- The Otsu histogram never sends a rendered symbol's two values through memory. `histogram[value]++` serializes on store forwarding when consecutive pixels hit the same bin, and a rendered symbol is two values in long runs. The first fix folded eight equal pixels into one `+= 8` (8–10× on the images it was measured on, while the textbook multi-lane fix managed ~2.4×), but those images were 8 px/module in a width that is a multiple of eight, the one layout where every group of eight is uniform. The same two-valued symbol at 8.4 px/module cost 6× as much a pixel, 3 px/module almost never folds, and a smooth gradient, where neighbours share a bin, ran at 1.56 ns a pixel against 0.09.

  The 256-bit tier (net8.0+, `Binarizer.FillHistogramVector256`) compares 32 pixels against 0 and against 255, counts the two masks in registers, and sends only the other pixels to the bins, so a two-valued block costs the same wherever its boundaries fall. A block that is mostly other values goes to the scalar groups, and after two blocks in a row with neither counted value, the next 31 are taken without the test. The x64 threshold stage at version 40 went 274 → 14 µs at 3.4 px/module, 442 → 22 at 4.4 px, 1,209 → 83 at 8.4 px, 193 → 75 in the 8 px aligned best case, 357 → 115 rotated at 4 px and 844 → 249 on a no-symbol gradient. Image decode went 549 → 204, 797 → 241, 1,594 → 392, 463 → 337, 716 → 523 and 1,741 → 555 µs. Every bin is identical on every tier (`OtsuHistogramParityTest`, each tier entered directly), so the threshold and the grey levels are too.

- That tier was 8 to 11 % slower on photo-like images, which an end-to-end A/B found after the kernel benchmark had shown the opposite. The benchmark's baseline was the shipped loop copied verbatim but taking the histogram as a span parameter, where the library's is a `stackalloc int[256]` in the same method. The JIT knows that length and drops the bounds check of every `histogram[(byte)v]`, while the copy paid the check per increment. So the copy was slower than the real code on noise (1.15×) and faster on gradients and two-valued images (0.25× to 0.73×), because the check spaced out same-bin increments. Every "against the shipped code" ratio from it was wrong in one direction or the other. Only the order between candidates held. A faithful copy is one whose disassembly matches, not one whose source does. The repair was the untested stretch above:
  - With the test in front of every block, a photo-like threshold measured +8 to +11 %.
  - With 7 untested blocks, +2 to +3 %.
  - With 31, level (0.97 to 1.03 over two runs, inside the harness's spread).
- These were measured and left out of that kernel.
  - Splitting the dense blocks' increments over 4 or 8 sub-histograms, four ways: a gradient gains 8 to 12 %, and noise and photo-like images lose 5 to 20 % to the extra L1 footprint.
  - A dense cut-over other than 12 (a block with more than 12 of its 32 pixels neither 0 nor 255 goes to the scalar groups): 20 measured the same, and 6 sent blocks rich in the two counted values back through memory and lost a third on resampled images.
  - A fast path for blocks that are wholly 0 and 255 gained 27 to 35 % on two-valued images and lost 4 to 17 % on resampled ones. It was unstable between runs, because the JIT lays the three paths out differently under each workload's profile, which C# cannot steer.
  - A 512-bit tier halved the 256-bit one's time on two-valued images. It was not shipped, because no CI runner is sure to execute it and it would be the library's only 512-bit tier.
  - In a 128-bit tier at 16 pixels a step, a gradient ran 1.85× slower than the scalar walk, with a dense path whose disassembly matched the 256-bit tier's instruction for instruction. Only keeping the 32-pixel cadence (two loads, paired masks) fixed that, and it was still 8 % behind on gradients. It would run on ARM64 and WASM, where the mask extraction costs something else entirely. ARM64 has had its own tier since (two entries below), and x64 without AVX and WebAssembly have run it since 2026-09-30, measured on those builds (below).
  - The scalar tier is the old walk through unchecked references: level on photo-like input, 0.24× to 0.72× on gradients and on resampled and unaligned two-valued images, 1.04× on the aligned best case. These are all x64 figures, for a tier x64 does not run. On ARM64 it measured 0.99 to 1.01 of the loop before it on every input.
- Where no other histogram tier runs, the 128-bit one does. x64 without AVX (a default NativeAOT publish) and WebAssembly counted in scalar. They now run the 256-bit tier's 32-pixel blocks on two 128-bit loads, with a movemask for each compare (`Binarizer.Vector128.cs`). The x64 JIT result above did not carry over. Against the scalar tier, the histogram alone on default NativeAOT, WebAssembly AOT and interpreted took 0.11, 0.09 and 0.16 on rendered version 40 at 3 px, 0.48, 0.31 and 0.51 rotated at 4 px, 0.93, 1.11 and 0.99 on a gradient, and 0.99 to 1.01 soft and on noise, except WebAssembly AOT at 1.04 and 1.07. Image decode, each shape in its own process, took 0.57, 0.60 and 0.79 at version 40 and 3 px, 0.99, 1.02 and 1.01 soft, and 1.01, 1.02 and 1.00 on the no-symbol gradient, inside each run's spread. WebAssembly keeps the tier for that. Moving the dense blocks' group walk out of the vector method lost: a call per dense block cost noise 24 to 35 %, and a call per untested stretch cost soft and noise 9 to 10 %.

- The halving has a tier for each build, and WebAssembly needed its own shift. `LuminanceHalver` (2026-10-11) reads each row's bytes as 16-bit lanes, so a lane holds a horizontal pair, the two rows add, and the means narrow back to bytes: 64 pixels of each row a step on 256-bit vectors, 32 on 128-bit ones, and four in a 64-bit word on the scalar tier, which also ends every row. The scalar tier alone over 12 megapixels: 1.6 ms on x64, where the first cut, a byte at a time, took 3.7. Each tier against the scalar one, the kernel alone on 740 px of noise and on 12 megapixels (the fastest of five, a quiet machine): x64 JIT with AVX2 0.16 and 0.23, without 0.18 and 0.21, a default NativeAOT publish 0.19 and 0.28, `x86-64-v3` 0.17 and 0.31, WebAssembly AOT 0.24 and 0.25 and interpreted 0.11 and 0.14. The 12-megapixel runs vary by a fifth to a half between their fastest and their median on x64, the buffers being larger than the cache of whichever core the process lands on, where the 740 px pair holds within 7 % on every build but the JIT with AVX2 (22 %). The portable 128-bit tier measured first on WebAssembly: interpreted 0.15 of scalar, compiled ahead of time 4.4 times scalar (268 µs against 60 at 740 px). Three copies with one operation each swapped for the platform's instruction found the shift: `Vector128.ShiftRightLogical` on 16-bit lanes compiles to a lane walk there, `PackedSimd.ShiftRightLogical` to the instruction (16.4 µs), and the narrowing swapped as well gives 14.4. So WebAssembly runs `LuminanceHalver.Wasm.cs`, the same step on the platform's shift and narrowing, dispatched ahead of the portable tier. The no-symbol shapes (740 px noise and a ramp), each build taken in turn with the build before, the fastest of eleven: 0.97 to 1.01 on noise and 0.89 to 0.97 on the ramp, the halving being about 8 % of the ramp. The search's own method compiles as before on every build read (the JIT on .NET 8 and 10 with and without AVX, ILC default and `x86-64-v3`: the same instructions, byte for byte on .NET 10), and the scalar tier's word loop is one instruction shorter than the shipped method's, its entry now a call. Seven faults planted in a copy were caught, one of them only once the tiers were held to their spans at a page end: a step one output pixel past the row wrote one byte past the destination and read two past the source, which no comparison of the halved image sees. The one not caught inverts the dispatch's first test, so an AVX2 machine runs the 128-bit tier: the output is the same, and the tier report takes a kernel's tier from the instruction sets and not from which method ran, the gap the 128-bit round recorded. On ARM64 (an Apple M2, the same day) the portable tier takes 0.21 to 0.22 of the word loop on the JIT of .NET 8 and 10 and on a default NativeAOT publish, 1.0 million cycles over 12 megapixels against the word loop's 4.7 million and a plain copy's 0.82, and its loop is the same 31 instructions on all three. At 2 % of a failing image there it is under the bar for a form on the platform's pairwise instructions, so none was built. The no-symbol images, counted in cycles with three builds in turn, take 0.93 to 1.00 of the word loop's, the gain the kernel pair predicts, where times between processes on that machine move more than the tiers do.

- ARM64 has its own histogram tier, built from what that core makes cheap. On an Apple M2 the scalar tier cost twice x64's per pixel wherever increments to one bin chain (1.47 ns on a 3 px render, 2.0 on a gradient), and the same on noise (0.31), which made the threshold 30 to 87 % of a version 40 image decode and the largest stage on every input. `Binarizer.FillHistogramAdvSimd` (net8.0+, `AdvSimd.Arm64`) keeps the 256-bit tier's blocks, on two 128-bit loads, and differs where ARM64 differs:

  - There is no movemask, and `ExtractMostSignificantBits` is a sequence here, four a block. A block's extremes are counted by one add across its two compare masks (each lane is 0, −1 or −2, so the byte sum is minus the count). The zeros accumulate in byte counters drained every 120 blocks. A mask of the other pixels, one bit a byte from a narrowing shift of the compare masked to 0x11, is built only for a sparse block that has any. The general-register popcount is a round trip through the vector unit on this core, and a block that is all 0 and 255 now takes none of these steps.
  - The dense blocks and the untested stretch count into four sub-histograms, pixel i of a group into lane i % 4. x64 refused this for its L1 footprint, but this core's 128 KB L1 holds it: lanes alone took a gradient to 0.22 and photo-like images to 0.82 of the scalar tier. Each lane is its own reference. Addressing lane k as one base plus 256·k made the JIT sign-extend the sum on the way to every load, and cost noise 14 %.
  - The lanes are rented from `ArrayPool` once a call: 4 KB is past the few hundred bytes the library allows on the stack.

  These were measured and refused: two and eight lanes (noise 1.14 at eight), a dense cut-over of 8 or 16 instead of 12, and the sparse walk spread over two lanes.

  The rental, a stack buffer and a 1.5 KB `ushort` form differed by 2 to 10 % in isolation, and by as much on inputs that never touch the lanes, so the difference was not the storage. The decode A/B below cleared the rental. The cause came out later (2026-09-23). The walk sits in its own method so the rental's try region does not reach the block loop, and under dynamic PGO the Tier1 caller inlined it back (4,168 bytes of code with the vector loop in it, against a call without PGO). Measured alone, that took noise to 1.33 and a soft render to 1.11 of the scalar tier. Switching PGO off, or giving the walk the same rental from another caller, put both back to 0.99 and 0.84. Inside a decode the caller is not profiled the same way, and the end-to-end numbers were level either way. The walk is marked `NoInlining`, because a method split meant to keep a loop out of a try region holds only if the JIT cannot undo it, and a FullOpts disassembly does not show what Tier1 does.

  Inside a decode on the M2 at version 40, the threshold stage went 455 → 14 µs at 3 px/module, 559 → 18 at 3.4 px, 2,110 → 103 at 8.4 px, 465 → 93 on the 8 px aligned render and 704 → 335 rotated at 4 px, took 0.79 to 0.88 photo-like, went 1,097 → 243 on a no-symbol gradient, and was level on noise. Image decode (stage harness, median of three alternating passes) took 0.19 to 0.54 at version 40 on rendered symbols, 0.49 to 0.85 rotated and 0.86 to 0.96 photo-like, 0.22 to 0.97 at versions 6 to 20 by the same classes, 1.00 on no-symbol noise, and 0.29 and 0.42 on the gradient. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry, two runs a side), version 40 at 3 px went 720 → 267 µs, at 3.4 px 859 → 306, rotated 4 px 1,139 → 754, soft 4 px 554 → 525, the version 6 URL 34.1 → 15.4, no-symbol noise 3,304 → 3,318 (level), and the gradient 1,127 → 317. Through the shared threshold, Micro QR M4 went 11.4 → 6.4 µs, rMQR R7x43 12.8 → 7.0 and R17x139 67.6 → 34.7, and rMQR no-symbol noise 8,012 → 7,677 and gradient 145 → 124. Allocated was unchanged, with the span rows at zero. `OtsuHistogramParityTest` enters the tier directly, with inputs long enough to drain the counters many times, and with a call after a noise image that would show lanes left uncleared.

- Whether the grey levels are enabled is a statement about the bins, and it is now made in integers. `GreyLevels.FromHistogram` disables the levels when no pixel lies strictly between the two class means, since every share is then 0 or 1 and says nothing the threshold did not. The scan for such a pixel was bounded by the float means, and a float loses a weighted sum's low bits past 2²⁴, which for a light class at 255 is 65,794 pixels. Past that the mean rounds to 255.00001, the scan reaches bin 255 itself, and whether a pure two-valued image gets the near-miss second look depends on its pixel count: a 555 × 555 render of a version 40 symbol at 3 px/module got it, and the same symbol at 3.4 px did not. A kernel benchmark's gate found this because its scenes reproduced it. The bounds are now the smallest bin above the dark mean and the largest below the light mean, from the integer sums (floor + 1 and ceil − 1), exact at any count. The levels, the scale and the minimum-range check keep their float form.

  `GreyLevelsEnableTest` covers two-valued histograms at seven level pairs and counts from 1 to 4 million, one pixel between at the same counts, the darkness readings and the range check. It also covers the bounds where they are tightest: a pixel in the bin next to either level or next to a class mean that is not a whole number, a class whose count reaches exactly half its weight, and levels exactly the minimum range apart. No decode fixture moved, because on a two-valued image the strict ratio finds the finders and the second look had nothing to add.

- The inverted retry does not count the negative. A pixel of value v is 255 − v in the negative, so the negative's histogram is the first polarity's with bin i at 255 − i. The image decode passes all three image decoders share (`ImageDecodePasses`) count once and, before the retry, reverse the bins in place (`Binarizer.InvertHistogram`). The threshold and the grey levels come from `ComputeOtsuThresholdFromHistogram` either way. The threshold is searched again on the mirrored bins, not mirrored itself, because the search keeps the first of equal splits and two values with nothing between them tie at every split, so on a rendered symbol, exactly that case, `256 − threshold` would be a different threshold. Only an image not read in its first polarity is affected. On x64 a no-symbol gradient went 530 → 287 to 309 µs at 740 × 740 and 1,863 → 1,045 at 1480 × 1480, noise 2,666 → 2,561 and 6,136 → 5,520 (the finder search is the rest), and Micro QR and rMQR on a 400 × 400 gradient 155 → 93. Decodes that succeed are level. The existing inverted-decode tests could not see the wiring, because on pure black and white the unmirrored bins give a threshold that also splits the negative. `OtsuInvertedHistogramTest` reads a light-on-dark symbol with modules at 150 on 25 through each decoder and checks the mirrored bins' threshold and grey levels against a per-pixel count of the negative.

- A scan holds one module buffer at a time, or the pool's shared stacks decide whether it allocates.
  - Each grid attempt used to rent its own buffer, so a dimension could have three buffers of one size out at once (the first sampling, another grid compared against it, and a coverage re-read).
  - The array pool keeps one array a size per thread, so the second and third came from per-core stacks every thread shares. With other tests decoding beside it, the failure path allocated 4,120 B in every round, in one of six runs on .NET 8. Alone it never did.
  - Since 2026-09-29 a scan rents one array of three grids for the largest dimension it has sampled (`ModuleWorkspace`), again only for a larger one.
  - `DecodeAllocationTest` checks the peak count of buffers out at once per image (`QRImageDecoder.ModuleBuffersPeak`). Before the change that count was 2 or 3 on the bowed symbol, the next triple and noise.
  - The inverted image's buffer is still out during the negative pass, and a module buffer of the same size bucket then still comes from the shared stacks.
  - The reads measured 0.3 to 1.3 % slower in the fastest of twelve alternating runs (version 6 at 4 px/module, 9.75 to 9.88 µs), the failing images within 0.6 %. Without the counters, and with the workspace renting one grid instead of three, the reads were still 0.5 to 1.0 % slower, so neither is the cause. It was not traced further.
- A workspace passed by `ref` beside spans must not be a `ref struct`. The compiler refuses a `ref ModuleWorkspace` argument next to a stack-allocated span, or next to an `ImageView` built from a local passed by `in` (CS8350), because a ref struct's fields could capture either.
  - The workspace holds only an array and a length, so it is a plain struct.

### Measuring and verifying a hot-path change

These lessons come from the matrix decode round of 2026-09-20 and 21 (codeword extraction, the bit stream reader, the ARM syndrome kernel) and the image round of 2026-09-21 to 23 (the threshold fill, the mesh sampler, the finder search, and their ARM64 tiers). None is about the decoder itself, and each cost a wrong conclusion or nearly did.

- Look for the inverse of an existing table before designing a kernel. Both tables that made extraction fast had been built by the encoder for the opposite direction, and the decoder was already loading them to read one field.
- A cache of something periodic is a table of its period. Asking what the mask bits under one output byte depend on turned a per-version mask stream, 441 KB worst case, into 1,152 bytes for every version.
- Sharing a table with the encoder removes the cross-check a round trip used to give, because both sides would be wrong together. The independent reference walk and the third-party fixtures replace it, and the reference must stay off the shared tables.
- Check parity on a dirty buffer. The reference walk ORs into a cleared buffer and the run walk stores, so a comparison on a buffer of zeros would have passed either way. Comparing on a buffer filled with 0xA5 allowed the clear in `DecodeMatrix` to go.
- An exit criterion is a claim about the format and is checked like one. "Level L and H end the stream in different places" sounded right and tested nothing, because data plus ECC is one total per version. The cut is driven by shortening the output instead.
- A prediction is not a reason. "The smaller footprint will win on ARM64" was written as the reason for a choice, but the measuring machine had less L1 than the target, and the target later reproduced the x64 ordering exactly. The choice rested on memory alone, which needed no second machine.
- A mutation run starts from a baseline that shows the expected count. A TUnit tree filter of the form `/*/*/(A|B)/*` matched no test and still printed `failed: 0`, so twelve planted faults looked like twelve survivors. The baseline line printing `succeeded: 0` gave it away. Run one class per invocation.
- When the red is a missing method, add it in the old style first, because a compile error says nothing about the tests around it. With `ReadBytes` added as a bit loop, the new tests ran against the old reader and split into new contract (seven) and characterization (the rest) by measurement rather than argument.
- An equivalent mutant is a question about the code, not a gap in the tests. The one survivor of the reader round was an explicit return that a later check also covers. It stayed, because seeing that takes an inequality the reader of the code should not need, and the decision is recorded beside the rule it concerns.
- Carry two arms of identical code. On the M2 their spread (0.0 to 1.6 %) made a 24 % gap conclusive, for the cost of one enum value.
- An isolated stage is a hint, and only one call site is real. The bit stream stage measured 7 and then 13 µs from two builds of one harness while the end-to-end figure did not move, and the shipped syndrome kernel measured 94, 148, 198 and 99 ns a block from four call sites. Ratios are compared between candidates on one call site. The quoted figure is the end-to-end A/B, built from an export of the committed tree against the working tree, with the binaries checked to differ.
- A capability-gated test is evidence only on a machine with the capability. `GetCoreData` was routed through a kernel whose AdvSimd parity test had been skipped on every x64 run of two phases. It first executed on the M2, a day after it shipped.
- A second back end changes what is left, not what won. ARM64 reproduced every kernel ordering, but a stage the x64 profile had ruled out of scope at 2 % became the second largest there, at 28 %.
- Open the file before writing the hypothesis. The plan contained a guess about the ARM syndrome kernel that one minute in the source refuted: the kernel's own comment named the real cost.
- Count what a change is meant to reduce before timing it. The run caps were planned on a measurement of 32 pixels walked for a 21 pixel window, taken to mean that walks ran long. Counted per run, the cap as planned saved 15 % and the centre-first walk that replaced it 40 to 45 %, both known before either existed as library code. The count of pixels read does not depend on the machine's load, and at 8 px/module, where every read is a cache line, it is the cost.
- The minimum over passes rewards the luckiest pass. One pass in six of one binary measured 118 µs where the other five measured 163 to 174, and the minimum made that arm look 1.15× better than the arm it lost to in every other pass. Rounds inside a pass share the machine's state. Passes do not. Across alternating passes the figure is the median, and three passes is the fewest that have one.
- Time the stages before the second hypothesis, not after it. The first vector form of the row kernel halved the walk. The two ideas for the rest (the extraction loop's branches, the classification's instruction count) were both wrong, and each took a full benchmark round to find out. Three probes that stop the kernel after each stage then measured 12 % mask, 29 % extraction, 36 % classification and 23 % hit handling. That split showed why a variant that halved the classification had gained nothing (its extraction had grown by as much), and every variant written from it was confirmed.
- Verify a code generation switch in the disassembly. The check that the kernel's ranking holds without AVX-512 first ran with `DOTNET_EnableAVX512F=0`, which .NET 10 ignores (it reads `DOTNET_EnableAVX512=0`). The run reproduced the previous round and would have passed for the answer. Counting mask-register instructions in the exported disassembly, 1,435 and then none, told the two runs apart.
- An isolated stage is a floor, and the sum of floors under-reads the whole. Seven stages of an image decode, each looped alone, summed to 328 µs against a decode of 442 (version 40, 4 px/module, x64), because a stage on its own runs with its part of the image in cache, and in a decode it does not. One arm that runs the stages back to back in one body measured within 3 % of the decode on 33 of 34 inputs. Shares are stated as shares of the decode, and a stage's own figure is a lower bound.
- A benchmark shape at a whole number of pixels per module measures an alignment. The threshold's uniform-group fold was fast only where module boundaries land on multiples of eight pixels, and the same two-valued symbol at 8.4 px/module cost 6x as much a pixel. Every image class now includes a fractional pitch beside the whole ones, and a variant is judged on the fractional, soft and rotated classes first and on the hard renders last.
- Ask the count first. The first question put to the image profile was how many times `SampleAndDecode` runs, and the answer was once on every input. Asking that first justified reading every other column as the cost of a decode rather than of a search. Had the answer been two, it would have ended the round.
- The end-to-end A/B per input class is a detector, not a confirmation. The first histogram tier measured 0.24x to 0.90x on every other class and +8 to +11 % on all nine photo-like inputs, which the kernel benchmark had shown as a win. One class with nine inputs, all of the same sign, separated it from noise, where a single "image decode" number would have averaged it away. The repair took three measured steps, and the first made it worse.
- A surviving mutant that tightens a bound is a statement about the bound. Three faults that lowered the cross-check's centre bound by one survived an exhaustive test of the bound against the verdict, so the derived bound has a pixel of slack. Asking the same question of the formula before the sweep found two terms that could never bind. The derivable bound was kept, at the cost of a pixel.
- A change that gains nothing can be what a gaining change needs. The edge list alone and the integer ratio alone measured level with the row walk, but the branch-free kernel could not be written without either. A variant's verdict is about that variant as an end point, so a series of variants keeps its refuted steps.
- The rows a change cannot reach show whether an end-to-end class can be trusted. One Micro QR run measured its PNG generation rows, identical in both trees, 1.5x slower on the changed side in both passes, and its decode row slower with them. Run again with the order reversed, everything was level. Those rows were looked at only because the decode row looked wrong. Now they are read first.
- A stage probe can miss what the stage does to its neighbours. The edge extraction alone measured level three times, while the row pass it sits in measured 5 to 15 % faster with the one-loop form. The change was one branch per pair of edges, and the classification and flagged-window loops of the same row share the branch predictor with it, so a branch change is judged inside the loop it shares the predictor with.
- A refutation belongs to the machine it was made on. Four sub-histogram lanes were refused four times on x64 for their L1 footprint, and they are the whole gain on gradients and photo-like images on a core with four times the L1. The movemask, the sixteen-window step and the bit extraction of the x64 row kernel each had to be replaced on ARM64, while its structure transferred whole. The record says why a variant lost, because the reason is what may not transfer.
- A warmup that is enough on one machine is not evidence on another. The stage harness's 60 ms had been enough on x64 but left the M2 at Tier0, where a version 40 decode measured 900 µs, and 715 once warmed for 300 ms. A stage figure that moves when the warmup doubles is not valid.
- Restoring a planted fault by moving a backup back keeps the faulted binary. `mv` restores the old timestamp, so the incremental build sees nothing to do. The run after the last fault stayed red until the file was touched. A mutation sweep has not ended until it ends with a rebuilt, counted green baseline.
- Two copies of the benchmark project build none. The benchmark host found a second copy under a worktree in `.claude/` and refused to build, and the first end-to-end pass wrote NA rows without failing its script. Both trees of an A/B are now exported outside the repository, and the script stops on a build refusal.
- Instructions a call name the change that added work, where cycles and time only suggest it. Between two builds that ran the same instructions a shape's cycles moved by up to 5 % on NativeAOT and 4 % on the JIT, the code landing elsewhere. Counted from the process, a short loop taken from a long one, instructions repeated to four digits and put every step of nine commits on the one that made it.
- A loop's registers are a budget, and an edit to a hand-written tier is read in its loop on each compiler, as its speed was when it was written. The mesh sampler's third node meant two more table references live across the loop. What does not fit the registers the JIT keeps on the frame and loads every pass, and on ARM64 those loads were 18 of the 42 instructions the edit added.
- A cost moved to another class is measured on that class. Asking for the version read at the finders only after the estimate's grid had failed took it off every clean symbol, and the 15 lens shots it exists for took 1.15 to 3.26 times as long, a failed sampling ahead of each. Asking the symbol whether it states the estimate, 36 pixels through the frame already built, took it off the same clean symbols and left the lens shots their path (2026-10-13).

- Code the decode path never runs can still slow the method it is written into. Holding the reference walk to the bounded walk's limits was one more condition in the cross-check's reference branch, which only the parity tests' entry takes, and BoofCV's photographs read 3 % slower in sum, 4.5 % on the 12-megapixel ones. In a method of its own, not inlined, they read 1.3 % faster than before the change, which is what the change itself was worth. The frame was not looked at.

- A conversion at a rarely run call is not inlined, and every call of the method pays for it. A build that added five cold calls, each converting `Span<byte>` to `ReadOnlySpan<byte>`, decoded a Standard QR Byte symbol 2.5 to 3.5 % slower with nothing new on its path: the bit-stream decoder's frame grew from 536 to 648 bytes and its prolog zeroed the frame in a loop. Converted once, where the bytes are read, the frame is 552 bytes and the times are back.
- A tier written for one architecture is checked against the portable one on that architecture. The 128-bit mesh tier was written after the ARM64 one, as its steps on portable vectors, and had only been timed on the builds with no other tier. On ARM64 it compiles to nearly the same loop and takes 0.96 to 1.00 of the ARM64 tier's cycles, 0.98 as NativeAOT code, so the ARM64 tier was removed (2026-10-13).
- Code written beside a hot path is held to the hot path's own listings, and the pools are part of them. The entry that returns every symbol is new files only, so that the one-symbol call runs the instructions it ran (2026-10-14). On the .NET 10 JIT for x64, the 446 library methods compiled while the report's image and matrix shapes decode came out instruction for instruction the same, the number of a string literal's token aside. On a default NativeAOT publish for x64, ILC's map file gives each method's length and hash, and all 9,171 methods of the build before are byte for byte the same in the build after. The first build was not: its candidate list was rented from a pool of its own element type, the runtime gained a pool, and `Rent`, `Return` and the thread's bucket setup of every other pool came out the same length with other bytes. The list is rented as bytes. ARM64 and WebAssembly were not compared.
- A probe times nothing until every operation in it has reached its last tier. Timed after its own warm-up alone, a probe's first operation read 630 ns in two trees against BenchmarkDotNet's 127, the methods it shares with the others still instrumented. All operations are warmed, then all are timed.

### Measuring an accuracy change

These lessons come from the rounds measured against other readers (2026-09-21 to 28, all three decoders, and 2026-10-10 to 12, Standard QR on photographs. The rules are in [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#image-decode-sweep)). Each cost a wrong conclusion or nearly did.

- Diagnose stage by stage from the input the decode had. A probe called `EstimateModules` and added the 7 modules the function already counts, giving round, plausible causes (a version or two off for two renders, 8 to 11 modules long for 24 others) that went into the record unchecked. Taken the decoder's way, the two counted within 1.2 modules of the dimension and the 24 within 3.2. A number a probe derives is a claim about the code only once the probe does what the code does.
- Switch each piece off alone on the final code, over every set. Two pieces that were exact in theory changed nothing and were removed (the dimension from each line's sizes, the frame's mesh seeds), and one that looked minor, the timing match through the frame, was worth 47 of 400 at 40-50 % keystone. A piece removed for changing nothing may have been hidden by a stage in front of it: the dimension from each line came back, worth 20 renders, once the stretched finder was found. After the last change to an order, the parts are measured again and the renders the tests check are chosen again.
- "Nothing lost over every set" is about the sets. A cut that removes a fallback needs the case the fallback exists for, built on purpose. Skipping the full sweep in the regional attempt lost nothing on any set measured, because the sets that turn or offset a symbol were evenly lit and the unevenly lit one was axis-aligned. On the purpose-built case it lost 30 to 47 of each 880. A renderer hides a stage the same way: none drew the top-left finder nearest until the two-axis tilt did, and the first thing that tilt broke was the corner, a stage nobody suspected.
- A regression render must keep needing its mechanism when nudged, and still read around the point. Renders chosen as red before and green after did not tell the centroid from the coverage reading, since either alone read many of them, so each case is chosen with its own mechanism switched off. An exact tie, such as a right-angle turn at a half-pixel offset, tests the rounding and not the geometry. A robustness claim states the grid it was checked on, or checks densely: a 20-nudge search passed renders that failed between its nudges. The grids the test renders were chosen on:
  - `KeystoneFinderDecodeTest`: every decode render was chosen from a search to fail on the commit before, to fail with its own mechanism switched off, and to hold under nudges of turn ±0.5°, density ±0.02 and keystone ±0.005. Two are exceptions. The second alternative-triple render reads at one nudge of seven with that piece off. The render whose first alternative is false holds its premise at its exact parameters only, as its assertions check.
  - `SmallLatticeMeshDecodeTest`: one bowed render a version, each failing on the commit before and reading under nudges of ±0.05 px/module, ±0.5° and ±0.05 module of bow.
  - `SpreadRingDecodeTest`: each render fails on the commit before and reads under nudges of ±0.05 px/module, ±0.5° and ±0.01 of a module.
- A test asserts its premises both ways: which pass reads the case, that the other attempts fail, and that the strided scan finds nothing. Without those, a later change that reads the case earlier leaves the test green and guarding nothing. When a premise becomes false because the change did its job, the test moves to a case whose premise holds. It is not loosened.
- A bound checked on the test's own symbol is a bound on that symbol. The first failure under a shadow sat two versions from the symbol tested. A reference written from the same description as the code shares its boundaries, so a parity test guards only a boundary its inputs sit on.
- Measure a failure-path gate in the unit its cost is paid in, on the benchmark's own images too. "A grid got past its format information" was rare on the renders a retry was for and true of half of all grids on texture. Completing the stride pass's list cost nothing on one noise generator and doubled the cost on the benchmark's, because the stride pass's early return depends on the texture. Where a fallback sits decides who pays: inside each attempt, the midpoint scan charged every symbol the regional pass reads, and last in the order it charges only the images nothing else reads.
- A fix proposed with a finding is a hypothesis of its own. The regional pass had no negative, and the repair suggested with that finding, inverting the positive's output, read 2 of 48 such renders, where binarizing the negative's own pixels read 44.
- One flag summarizing several measurements is the premise of every rule that reads it. Set by the first failed walk, it stopped describing the sizes measured before that walk. A test case that cannot tell the repair from the defect (crossings on half pixels, equal to the runs, at 0°) is found only by running the defect.
- Read a lead from another reader's code up to the call that gates it. A ring-closure check looked like a detector of its own, but it runs only after four run checks pass, both diagonals at a tolerance this decoder refuses below 2.25 px/module. A lead aimed at renders past the yardstick has to prove itself on real images, or as a check of shipped code.
- Work written from renders of an earlier commit must find them again before it is built. Reading the version through the first transform was written for renders from three changes earlier, and a classification of the failures on the day found none of that kind.
- A check that saves only cost is tested by what the decoder does. Trying other corners without the timing check first changes no result and doubled a damaged symbol's failure time, so a test sees it through a recording stand-in for the steps a corner is tried with.
- A surviving mutant whose substitution never applied looks like dead code. Two survivors of one round were a CRLF file the substitution missed and a pattern whose check matched another line. Re-run after checking that the file changed, one of them was the bound the tests needed most. Mutants and red checks run in a scratch copy of the tree.
- A correct bound can still be the cost. The first like-edge side cap, derived from one distance, was correct but let every column walk a third of the centre past the ratio's own cap, most of a 4 to 5 % read cost. The exact maxima of the conditions, from a small linear program, removed it. Switching one part off at a time found it where timing the whole change could not.
- A stage's cost on what already reads is measured on shapes that read, not only on photographs. Eight stages each recorded 0.94 to 1.00 in sum on the photographs that read before, and together they cost a clean version 40 symbol 5 % in instructions and a bowed one 9 % (Performance). Most photographs are small versions, which never reach the version read, and a dense clean symbol is where the data offers the row scan candidates. The no-symbol shapes were timed for every change to a failure path, and nothing for the other path.
- A piece that only refuses is measured by switching it off, and a piece of the read by running it twice. Switched off, the sampler or the mesh builder sends a bowed symbol down another path, and the difference is that path's. Run twice into the same spans it changes nothing but the count.
- A probe that carries another reader's rule says which of its techniques is the lead before anything is built. The module-space read written into a probe split 19 photographs three ways in one run, and a mesh prototyped in a probe against the camera's own positions chose its order, its prediction and its sampler as a line of counts over 2,720 renders in a minute.
- A probe that hands a method an optional argument changes what the method does. A trace gave the axis cross-check a buffer for its runs, which is how its small-crisp mode is asked for, and reported both rows beside a centre row as refused while the decoder read them.
- A planted fault has to be a fault at the sizes the tests draw. A window's least reach of one module changes nothing on versions 2 to 4, where an eighth of the dimension decides, and survived for that reason alone.
- A class is counted from the pass that holds it. Classified at the global pass alone, 17 of 40 gap photographs were short of a finder. Over every pass and scale, 14 of the 40 had the right triple and failed at the grid, which the first count hid.
- A photograph's grid is known from a corrected read, not from its text. Encoded again from the text read, a version 25 symbol matched the grid that read it on 71 % of its modules at every level, mask and segmentation, where a read with 80 corrections cannot be 5 % wrong.
- What a set does not hold, it does not show absent. No black-and-white render gained from the reduced-scale search, so such images were left out of it, and the photograph set had two.
